questionText: In animals dying of hepatic encephalopathy secondary to cirrhosis or portosystemic shunting, hyperammonemia induces a characteristic microscopic lesion in the cerebral cortex and basal ganglia consisting of:
options: Alzheimer Type II astrocytes and polymicrocavitation
Perivascular cuffs of eosinophils and Negri bodies
Neurofibrillary tangles and senile beta-amyloid plaques
Coagulative necrosis of Purkinje cells in the cerebellum
explanation: Astrocytes detoxify ammonia via glutamine synthetase; excess intracellular glutamine causes osmotic swelling of astrocytic nuclei into large, pale, vesicular 'Alzheimer Type II' nuclei appearing in pairs/triplets alongside spongy vacuolation (status spongiosus) at grey-white matter junctions.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency (EPI) presenting in young adult German Shepherd dogs with weight loss and voluminous pale steatorrhea is most commonly caused by:
options: Diffuse amyloidosis obliterating both pancreatic acini and beta cells
Chronic ascending trematode infection by Eurytrema pancreaticum
Congenital agenesis of the accessory pancreatic duct of Santorini
Immune-mediated pancreatic acinar atrophy sparing islets of Langerhans
explanation: In German Shepherds and Rough Collies, EPI is an inherited autoimmune disorder mediated by CD8+ T lymphocytes that selectively destroy zymogen-producing pancreatic acinar cells while completely sparing endocrine islets (no diabetes mellitus).

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In pigs, 'Mulberry Heart Disease' (dietary microangiopathy) is frequently accompanied in rapidly growing weaners by which fatal hepatic lesion?
options: Periportal fatty change with Mallory-Denk bodies
Multiple milk-spot fibrotic scars on Glisson's capsule
Diffuse biliary cirrhosis with pipe-stem calcification
explanation: Combined deficiency of Vitamin E and Selenium in growing pigs manifests as three classic syndromes: Mulberry Heart Disease (myocardial hemorrhage/microangiopathy), Hepatosis Dietetica (mosaic lobular hemorrhagic necrosis of the liver), and Nutritional Myopathy.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Progressive Atrophic Rhinitis in young growing pigs—characterized by complete resorption of the ventral scroll of the ventral nasal conchae (turbinates) and lateral deviation of the snout—is driven by a synergistic infection of:
options: Haemophilus parasuis and Streptococcus suis type 2
explanation: Bordetella bronchiseptica colonizes the nasal mucosa and causes initial turbinate hypoplasia, allowing toxigenic Pasteurella multocida (producing Pasteurella multocida toxin, PMT) to inhibit osteoblast differentiation and activate osteoclasts, resorbing the turbinate bones.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In horses with Guttural Pouch Mycosis (typically Aspergillus fumigatus), a thick diphtheritic mycotic plaque growing on the dorsomedial roof of the medial compartment commonly erodes which underlying artery, causing fatal epistaxis?
explanation: The internal carotid artery (and cranial nerves IX, X, XI, XII and cranial cervical ganglion) runs directly beneath the mucosa of the medial compartment of the equine guttural pouch; fungal invasion of the arterial wall causes mycotic aneurysm rupture and fatal epistaxis.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Why are cattle significantly more prone to obstructive atelectasis and poor resolution of bronchopneumonia compared to dogs and cats?
options: Bovine lungs possess complete fibrous interlobular septa
Bovine Type II pneumocytes fail to synthesize dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine surfactant
Bovine pulmonary arteries have no muscular tunica media to regulate perfusion
Bovine bronchioles completely lack Clara (club) cells and mucociliary escalators
explanation: Unlike canine and feline lungs—which have incomplete lobulation and abundant pores of Kohn providing collateral ventilation—bovine and porcine lungs have thick, complete interlobular connective tissue septa and lack pores of Kohn, so airway obstruction rapidly causes complete lobular atelectasis.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: At necropsy of a stillborn fetus vs a neonate that breathed before dying, forensic confirmation of 'atelectasis neonatorum' (stillbirth) is demonstrated when unfixed lung pieces:
options: Float in water and exude frothy blood-tinged surfactant upon incision
Float high on the surface of formalin due to putrefactive gas
Display prominent rib impressions and subpleural bullous emphysema
explanation: In congenital (fetal) atelectasis, alveoli have never expanded with air; the lungs are dark red, firm/fleshy (liver-like), have a specific gravity >1.00 (sink in water), and microscopically show slit-like alveolar spaces lined by prominent cuboidal pneumocytes.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Acute Bovine Pulmonary Edema and Emphysema (ABPEE / 'Fog Fever') occurring 4 to 10 days after adult cattle are moved from dry range to lush green aftermath pasture is caused by ruminal conversion of L-tryptophan into:
explanation: Ruminal Lactobacillus spp. convert excess dietary L-tryptophan in lush grass into indoleacetic acid and then 3-methylindole (3-MI); absorbed 3-MI is metabolized by cytochrome P450 (CYP4B1) in non-ciliated bronchiolar Clara (club) cells and Type I pneumocytes into pneumotoxic electrophiles, causing diffuse alveolar damage, hyaline membranes, and severe interstitial emphysema.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In classical lobar (croupous) pneumonia, why does the consolidated lung lobe change grossly from dark red ('red hepatization') to grey-brown ('grey hepatization') after 3 to 5 days?
options: Massive proliferation of anthracotic macrophages and fibroblasts in the pleura
Compression of septal capillaries by fibrinosuppurative exudate
Metastatic calcification of alveolar elastic fibers by parathyroid hormone
Complete replacement of alveolar spaces by hyperplastic Type II pneumocytes
explanation: During red hepatization, alveolar capillaries are engorged and alveoli contain erythrocytes and fibrin; in grey hepatization, rising intra-alveolar pressure from dense fibrin and leukocytes compresses septal capillaries (making the tissue bloodless/ischemic) while red cells lyse and hemoglobin is cleared.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Pyogranulomatous bronchopneumonia with large cavitary pulmonary abscesses combined with ulcerative pyogranulomatous typhlocolitis and mesenteric lymphadenitis in foals aged 1 to 5 months is pathognomonic for:
explanation: Rhodococcus equi is a facultative intracellular Gram-positive coccobacillus bearing the virulence plasmid VapA, which blocks phagosome-lysosome acidification inside alveolar macrophages; swallowing of coughed-up purulent sputum leads to ulcerative enterocolitis in ~50% of affected foals.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In cats, verminous pneumonia caused by the metastrongyloid lungworm Aelurostrongylus abstrusus is histopathologically distinguished by subpleural granulomas containing larvae and prominent:
options: Calcification of tracheal hyaline cartilage rings
Intranuclear eosinophilic inclusions inside bronchial goblet cells
Diffuse fibrinoid necrosis of the cranial vena cava
explanation: Aelurostrongylus abstrusus infection in cats (and toxocariasis/dirofilariasis) characteristically induces severe smooth muscle hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the media of small- and medium-sized pulmonary arteries along with hyperplasia of peribronchiolar submucosal glands.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In ruminants in sub-Saharan Africa, 'Heartwater'—characterized by massive straw-colored hydropericardium, hydrothorax, pulmonary edema, and clumps of rickettsial organisms inside brain capillary endothelial cells—is caused by:
explanation: Ehrlichia ruminantium (transmitted by Amblyomma ticks) multiplies inside endothelial cells of capillaries (readily demonstrated in cerebral cortex squash smears stained with Giemsa), causing severe vascular permeability and massive hydropericardium ('heartwater').

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In aged small-breed dogs (such as Miniature Poodles and Chihuahua) with severe chronic myxomatous mitral valve degeneration, sudden death with acute hemopericardium (cardiac tamponade) is frequently caused by:
options: Septic perforation of the tricuspid valve by Erysipelothrix
Dissecting aneurysm of the ascending pulmonary trunk
Full-thickness rupture of the dilated left atrium
Spontaneous rupture of a right auricular hemangiosarcoma
explanation: High-velocity regurgitant blood jets through an incompetent mitral valve strike the dilated left atrial endocardium (producing rough 'jet lesions'); acute rupture of chordae tendineae abruptly elevates left atrial pressure, tearing the weakened left atrial wall into the pericardial sac.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Why are dogs naturally resistant to spontaneous atherosclerosis unless they suffer concurrently from primary Hypothyroidism or Diabetes Mellitus?
options: Canine platelets do not synthesize platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF)
Dogs transport cholesterol predominantly in high-density lipoproteins
Canine vascular endothelium lacks scavenger receptors for oxidized lipoproteins
Dogs excrete 90% of dietary cholesterol directly through the renal glomeruli
explanation: Normal dogs are 'HDL-mammals' that carry most plasma cholesterol in cardioprotective HDL particles; only in severe hypothyroidism or diabetes mellitus does hypercholesterolemia shift cholesterol into atherogenic LDL/VLDL, causing yellow lipid-laden foam cell plaques in the tunica media and intima of coronary, renal, and cerebral arteries.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Unlike human intimal atherosclerosis, spontaneous canine atherosclerosis (secondary to hypothyroidism) histologically deposits lipid and cholesterol-laden foam cells predominantly within the:
options: Venous valves of the saphenous vein
explanation: In hypothyroid dogs, lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells) and smooth muscle cells accumulate heavily in the tunica media as well as the intima of coronary, thyroid, and cerebral arteries, transforming the vessels into rigid yellowish-white 'pipe-stem' cords.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC), an inherited autosomal dominant cardiac disease in Boxer dogs causing syncope and sudden ventricular fibrillation, is histologically characterized by:
options: Concentric hypertrophy of the left ventricular free wall with myofiber disarray
Fibrinoid necrosis of intramural coronary arterioles with mulberry hemorrhages
Endocardial fibroelastosis restricting diastolic filling of both ventricles
Atrophy of right ventricular cardiomyocytes with extensive fatty
explanation: Boxer ARVC (associated with striatin desmosomal gene mutations) features progressive myocyte loss and replacement of the right ventricular myocardium by adipose tissue or fibrofatty tissue.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: On transmission electron microscopy and Jones methenamine silver staining, 'Membranous Glomerulonephropathy' (the most common form of immune-complex glomerulonephritis in cats) is distinguished by:
options: Proliferation of parietal epithelial cells and fibrin filling Bowman's space to form crescents
Marked endothelial and mesangial cell proliferation with double-contour 'tram-track' splitting of the GBM
Diffuse thickening of glomerular capillary wall by subepithelial immune deposits separated by basement membrane 'spikes'
Complete fusion of podocyte foot processes without any electron-dense immune deposits
explanation: Membranous glomerulonephropathy involves in situ or planted immune complexes along the subepithelial aspect of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) without hypercellularity; newly synthesized GBM matrix grows between the deposits as argyrophilic 'spikes'.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In contrast, Type I Membranoproliferative (Mesangiocapillary) Glomerulonephritis—common in dogs with chronic infectious diseases like Dirofilariasis or Ehrlichiosis—shows a characteristic histological GBM pattern on silver or PAS stain described as:
options: Double-contour splitting of the glomerular basement membrane
Subepithelial spike-and-dome projections without mesangial hypercellularity
Hyaline nodular Kimmelstiel-Wilson glomerulosclerosis in the vascular pole
Diffuse linear anti-GBM IgG fluorescence along a thin basement membrane
explanation: In Membranoproliferative GN (MPGN), subendothelial immune complexes and proliferating mesangial cell processes interpose into the glomerular capillary wall, duplicating the basement membrane into a 'tram-track' (double-contour) configuration.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In neonatal foals aged 1 to 4 days dying of 'Sleepy Foal Disease', necropsy reveals multifocal pinpoint yellowish-white microabscesses distributed symmetrically throughout the renal cortices (embolic suppurative nephritis), caused by:
explanation: Actinobacillus equuli causes acute neonatal septicemia in foals ('sleepy foal disease'); bacterial emboli lodge in glomerular and peritubular capillaries, producing pathognomonic miliary microabscesses in the renal cortex and adrenal glands along with polyarthritis.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Why does acute nephrotoxic tubular necrosis (e.g., from gentamicin, mercuric chloride, or oak tannins) carry a much better prognosis for complete structural regeneration than ischemic (tubulorrhectic) acute tubular necrosis?
options: Nephrotoxic necrosis destroys proximal tubular epithelial cells but leaves tubular basement membrane intact as scaffold
Nephrotoxic necrosis induces immediate transdifferentiation of interstitial fibroblasts into podocytes
Ischemic necrosis affects only the collecting ducts in the renal crest
Nephrotoxins selectively destroy the glomerulus while sparing all renal tubules
explanation: Pure nephrotoxins kill proximal convoluted tubular epithelial cells uniformly while preserving the underlying tubular basement membrane (TBM) intact, allowing surviving tubular cells to flatten, divide, and re-epithelialize the nephron; ischemic ATN causes focal rupture of the TBM (tubulorrhexis), leading to tubular collapse and interstitial fibrosis.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In grazing cattle, seasonal consumption of large quantities of immature acorns and oak buds (Quercus spp.) causes acute renal failure, perirenal edema, and hydrothorax due to proximal tubular necrosis induced by:
explanation: Oak leaves and acorns (Quercus spp.) contain high levels of hydrolyzable tannins (gallotannins) that are converted in the rumen into gallic acid and pyrogallol, which bind proteins and cause severe coagulative necrosis of the proximal convoluted renal tubules.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In dehydrated horses and dogs treated with high doses of Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (such as phenylbutazone), selective coagulative ischemic necrosis of the renal crest (renal papillary necrosis) occurs because NSAIDs block synthesis of:
options: Vasoconstrictive thromboxane A2 (TXA2) in the afferent glomerular arteriole
Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) receptors on medullary collecting ducts
Vasodilatory prostaglandin E2 and prostacyclin in the renal medulla
Erythropoietin by peritubular interstitial fibroblasts in the renal cortex
explanation: The renal medulla and crest receive a low blood flow via the vasa recta and depend critically on local vasodilatory prostaglandins (PGE2 and PGI2) to maintain perfusion during hypovolemia; COX inhibition by phenylbutazone causes unopposed angiotensin/catecholamine vasoconstriction and ischemic papillary necrosis.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Why are Dalmatian dogs uniquely predisposed to forming radiolucent ammonium urate uroliths despite possessing normal hepatic levels of the enzyme uricase (urate oxidase)?
options: They have an inherited deficiency of xanthine oxidase in the renal proximal tubule
They have autosomal recessive mutation in SLC2A9 urate transporter blocking hepatic uptake
Their urine is persistently alkaline (pH > 8.5) due to defective distal tubular proton pumps
They synthesize excessive amounts of uric acid from dietary purines in the cecal mucosa
explanation: All Dalmatians are homozygous for a missense mutation in the SLC2A9 membrane urate transporter; although uricase is present inside hepatocyte peroxisomes, circulating uric acid cannot enter hepatocytes to be converted to allantoin and is also poorly reabsorbed by renal tubules.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In range steers and rams grazing native western prairie grasses during autumn and winter, hard, radiopaque, white-to-brown uroliths featuring multiple spiky radial projections ('jackstone' calculi) obstructing the sigmoid flexure are composed of:
explanation: Mature prairie grasses contain up to 4–8% dry weight plant opal (silica); absorbed silicic acid concentrates in the acidic, low-volume urine of water-deprived range steers and polymerizes with mucoproteins into classic 'jackstone' silica calculi that lodge at the sigmoid flexure or vermiform appendage.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In male Dachshunds, English Bulldogs, and Newfoundlands, flat, colorless, hexagonal ('benzene-ring') uroliths that precipitate specifically in acidic urine result from a hereditary proximal tubular defect in reabsorbing:
options: Dibasic amino acids including cystine, ornithine, lysine
explanation: Cystinuria is an inherited defect in the rBAT/b0,+AT dibasic amino acid transporter in the proximal convoluted tubule; while ornithine, lysine, and arginine are highly soluble, cystine is poorly soluble in acidic urine and precipitates as hexagonal crystals and calculi.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In dogs receiving long-term therapy with Allopurinol (for leishmaniasis or urate urolithiasis prevention) or in sheep grazing molybdenum-deficient pastures, yellowish-brown concentric uroliths may form composed of:
explanation: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase (a molybdenum-requiring metalloenzyme that converts hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid); enzyme inhibition or molybdenum deficiency causes accumulation and urinary precipitation of insoluble xanthine.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In horses fed corn contaminated with the fungus Fusarium verticillioides (F. moniliforme), fatal Equine Leukoencephalomalacia ('Moldy Corn Poisoning') with massive liquefaction and cavitation of subcortical cerebral white matter is caused by:
options: Aflatoxin B1 inhibiting nuclear RNA polymerase II
Satratoxin G inhibiting ribosomal peptidyl transferase
explanation: Fumonisin B1 is a structural analogue of sphinganine that competitively inhibits ceramide synthase, depleting complex sphingolipids (myelin) and accumulating toxic free sphinganine, which leads to vascular endothelial injury and liquefactive necrosis of cerebral white matter in equids.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In horses chronically grazing Yellow Star Thistle (Centaurea solstitialis) or Russian Knapweed (Acroptilon repens), fixed facial grimacing and inability to prehend food ('Chewing Disease') is caused by bilateral symmetrical necrosis of the:
options: Medullary obex, dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, and pons
Hippocampal pyramidal neurons (Ammon's horn) and amygdala
Cerebellar Purkinje cell layer and fastigial nuclei
explanation: Sesquiterpene lactones (such as repin) in Yellow Star Thistle cause oxidative dopamine-related neurotoxicity in horses, producing sharply demarcated foci of yellow-brown softening and cavitation restricted to the globus pallidus and substantia nigra.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In ruminants, Polioencephalomalacia (cerebrocortical necrosis) can be induced not only by thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency or ruminal thiaminases, but also by high dietary or water intake of which mineral?
explanation: Ruminal sulfate-reducing bacteria reduce excess dietary/water sulfur into toxic hydrogen sulfide (H2S) gas; inhaled/absorbed sulfide inhibits neuronal cytochrome c oxidase in the high-energy-demanding deep laminae of the cerebral cortex, producing laminar cortical necrosis identical to thiamine deficiency.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In neonatal and young lambs born to ewes grazing copper-deficient pastures (or high-molybdenum/high-sulfur pastures), progressive hindlimb ataxia ('Enzootic Ataxia' or 'Swayback') is characterized histopathologically by:
options: Suppurative microabscesses and mononuclear cuffing in the brainstem medulla
Bilateral symmetrical demyelination of spinal cord white matter tracts
Fibrinoid necrosis of spinal meningeal arteries with thrombosis
Intracytoplasmic eosinophilic Negri-like inclusions in lumbosacral motor neurons
explanation: Copper deficiency during mid-to-late gestation impairs fetal cytochrome c oxidase and phospholipid/myelin synthesis, producing symmetrical Wallerian-like degeneration and demyelination of dorsolateral (spinocerebellar) and ventromedial (motor) tracts of the spinal cord alongside chromatolysis of red/vestibular nuclei and cerebral white matter cavitation.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In foxes, mink, and cats fed diets rich in raw freshwater fish (such as carp or smelt) containing heat-labile thiaminase, 'Chastek Paralysis' is characterized histologically by bilateral symmetrical hemorrhagic necrosis of:
options: Dorsal root ganglia and sciatic peripheral nerve myelin sheaths
Cerebellar molecular layer and external germinal matrix
Subcortical cerebral white matter and corpus callosum
explanation: Unlike ruminants (where thiamine deficiency produces laminar cerebrocortical necrosis), carnivores (cats, dogs, foxes, mink) with thiamine deficiency develop selective bilateral symmetrical spongiosis, hemorrhage, and neuronal necrosis in brainstem periventricular grey nuclei, especially the caudal colliculi.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In sheep surviving the acute phase of Clostridium perfringens Type D enterotoxemia, epsilon toxin binds endothelial receptors in the brain, producing a subacute lesion known as:
explanation: Epsilon prototoxin (activated by trypsin) binds microvascular endothelial cells in the ovine brain, causing perivascular proteinaceous edema (microangiopathy) and bilateral symmetrical malacia in the internal capsule, basal ganglia, thalamus, and cerebellar peduncles (Focal Symmetrical Encephalomalacia).

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Following transection or crushing of a peripheral nerve axon, the sequential retrograde reaction occurring in the parent neuronal cell body (soma)—characterized by swelling, rounding of the perikaryon, eccentric displacement of the nucleus, and dispersion of Nissl substance from the center—is termed:
explanation: Central chromatolysis ('axonal reaction') represents dispersion and reorganization of rough endoplasmic reticulum (Nissl granules) in the central soma as the neuron shifts its metabolic machinery toward synthesizing structural proteins to regenerate the severed axon.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In young bitches following whelping, persistent serosanguineous vaginal discharge lasting for weeks to months due to failure of trophoblast-like cells to regress and continued invasion of the endometrium and myometrial arteries is termed:
explanation: In SIPS, fetal-origin syncytial/cytotrophoblast-like cells fail to degenerate after parturition and continue to erode maternal endometrial vessels, preventing normal vascular thrombosis and involution at the annular placental attachment zones.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In bovine mycotic abortion (most commonly caused by Aspergillus fumigatus entering hematogenously from mouldy hay via ruminal ulcers or lungs), the pathognomonic gross placental lesion is:
options: Thickened, leathery intercotyledonary placenta with necrotic 'cup-shaped' cotyledons
Bright cherry-red cotyledons with clean transparent intercotyledonary membranes
Thin, edematous placenta studded with pinpoint white calcified pearls on the amnion only
Complete liquefaction of caruncles into greenish-black foul-smelling pus
explanation: Aspergillus fumigatus causes necrotizing vasculitis of the placentomes; cotyledons become swollen with thickened, rolled margins enclosing necrotic caruncular tissue ('cup-shaped' or 'ringworm-like' cotyledons), and ~25% of aborted fetuses show raised greyish-white mycotic ringworm-like skin plaques.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In rams (especially associated with Brucella ovis infection or congenital blind efferent ductules), extravasation of spermatozoa into the interstitium of the epididymal head elicits an intense granulomatous foreign-body reaction ('sperm granuloma') in which spermatozoa stain:
options: Acid-fast bright red with Ziehl-Neelsen stain
Apple-green birefringent with alkaline Congo red
Turquoise-blue with Alcian blue at pH 2.5
Brilliant blue with Perl's Prussian blue iron stain
explanation: Mammalian sperm heads contain unique mycolic-like sulfoglycolipids and protamines that render extravasated spermatozoa strongly acid-fast on Ziehl-Neelsen staining, allowing histological identification of sperm granulomas even when sperm tails have lysed.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Histologically, acquired 'Testicular Degeneration' in an adult bull or stallion can be definitively differentiated from congenital 'Testicular Hypoplasia' because in Testicular Degeneration:
options: The tunica albuginea is replaced by metaplastic hyaline cartilage
Leydig interstitial cells are completely absent from the intertubular stroma
Seminiferous tubules are lined exclusively by neoplastic seminoma cells
Basement membrane of shrunken seminiferous tubules is thickened and wavy
explanation: In congenital testicular hypoplasia, tubules have never grown to normal size, so their basement membranes are thin and smooth; in acquired testicular degeneration/atrophy, previously expanded tubules collapse, leaving a redundant, wavy, buckled, and hyalinized basement membrane often accompanied by intratubular dystrophic calcification.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In equine acute laminitis (founder) triggered by grain overload or endotoxemia, separation of the interdigitating secondary epidermal lamellae from the dermal lamellae—allowing ventral rotation of the distal phalanx (P3)—is directly mediated by:
options: Direct bacterial invasion of the laminar corium by Fusobacterium necrophorum
Accumulation of monosodium urate crystals between the deep digital flexor tendon and navicular bone
Pathological activation of matrix metalloproteinases degrading basement membrane Type IV collagen
Autoimmune IgG antibodies targeting desmoglein-1 in the stratum spinosum of the hoof wall
explanation: In equine laminitis, systemic inflammatory mediators and hyperinsulinemia/ischemia activate constituent pro-MMP-2 and neutrophil-derived MMP-9 (gelatinases), which cleave hemidesmosome anchoring filaments and Type IV collagen of the laminar basement membrane, detaching the hoof wall from the pedal bone.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In aged horses with Pituitary Pars Intermedia Dysfunction (PPID / Equine Cushing's Disease), why do affected horses develop marked hirsutism (failure to shed a long, curly hair coat), hyperhidrosis, and polydipsia?
options: A primary functional adrenocortical carcinoma secretes excessive aldosterone and cortisol
Autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis destroys thyroid C-cells and lowers calcitonin
A functional corticotroph adenoma of the pars distalis secretes massive amounts of pure ACTH
explanation: Unlike canine Cushing's (usually a pars distalis ACTH adenoma), Equine PPID results from oxidative degeneration of hypothalamic dopaminergic neurons innervating the pars intermedia; loss of dopamine inhibition causes pars intermedia melanotrophs to proliferate and compress the hypothalamus while secreting POMC peptides (α-MSH, β-endorphin, CLIP, and ACTH).

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In dogs with untreated primary Hypothyroidism, accumulation of hyaluronic acid and chondroitin sulfate mucopolysaccharides in the dermis—which bind water to produce non-pitting facial thickening ('tragic facial expression')—is termed:
explanation: Thyroid hormone deficiency reduces catabolism of dermal glycosaminoglycans (hyaluronic acid); the hydrophilic mucin accumulates in the dermis (stained with Alcian blue), producing non-pitting mucinous skin thickening (myxedema) and a classic 'tragic' drooping facial expression.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In dairy cows suffering from acute Severe Coliform Mastitis (caused by Escherichia coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae), the dramatic systemic toxemia, fever, shock, and high mortality are primarily driven by:
options: Exotoxin-A ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor-2 inside alveolar secretory cells
Formation of chronic granulomatous sulfur granules blocking the teat cistern
Ascending invasion of bacteria directly into the iliac lymph nodes and vena cava
explanation: Coliform bacteria do not invade deep mammary parenchyma; rather, rapid multiplication and lysis of E. coli in milk releases massive amounts of lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin), causing acute necrotizing/hemorrhagic galactophoritis, vascular thrombosis, and endotoxic shock.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Chronic granulomatous mastitis in dairy cattle characterized by firm, tumor-like fibrotic nodules ('botryomycosis') containing tiny yellowish-white granules surrounded by eosinophilic Splendore-Hoeppli clubs is classically caused by:
explanation: Chronic granulomatous staphylococcal mastitis (mammary botryomycosis) is caused by Staphylococcus aureus; bacterial microcolonies in the udder become surrounded by eosinophilic antigen-antibody Splendore-Hoeppli material inside pyogranulomas encased in dense fibrous tissue.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In piglets under 4 weeks of age, 'Greasy Pig Disease' (Exudative Epidermitis)—characterized by generalized brown sebaceous-like greasy crusts, exfoliation, and dehydration without pruritus—is caused by exfoliative toxins of:
explanation: Staphylococcus hyicus produces exfoliative toxins (ExhA–D) that act as serine proteases specifically cleaving desmoglein-1 in the stratum granulosum of porcine epidermis, causing subcorneal clefting and exudation of serum and sebum ('greasy pig disease').

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In sheep, cattle, and horses, 'Dermatophilosis' ('Strawberry Footrot' or 'Lumpy Wool' / 'Rain Scald') is an exudative, crusting superficial dermatitis caused by an actinomycete whose diagnostic microscopic morphology in Giemsa-stained crust smears is:
options: Branching filaments dividing both transversely and longitudinally
Tightly coiled spirochetes demonstrable only under dark-field microscopy
Round yeast cells surrounded by a wide clear mucinous halo
explanation: Dermatophilus congolensis produces characteristic thick laminar paintbrush crusts consisting of alternating layers of parakeratotic keratin and degenerate neutrophils, within which branching filaments septate transversely and longitudinally into multidimensional 'railroad-track' tiers of coccoid zoospores.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In dogs and cats, a 'follicular cyst' vs 'epidermoid cyst' is distinguished from a true sebaceous gland adenoma because an epidermoid cyst is lined by stratified squamous epithelium and its lumen is filled with:
options: Fluid rich in cholesterol crystals and amylase
explanation: Epidermoid (infundibular) cysts arise from the hair follicle infundibulum, are lined by stratified squamous epithelium containing a granular cell layer (keratohyalin granules), and are filled with concentric laminated layers of flaky orthokeratotic keratin.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In chronic right-sided congestive heart failure or constrictive pericarditis, long-standing passive venous congestion of the liver leads to 'cardiac cirrhosis' (cardiac sclerosis), in which fibrous septa bridge specifically between:
options: Periportal Zone 1 sinusoids and lymphatic lacteals veins
Glisson's capsule and main hilar bile ducts veins
Adjacent portal triads while sparing central veins
explanation: In chronic passive hepatic congestion ('nutmeg liver'), severe hypoxia and sinusoidal hypertension in Zone 3 activate perisinusoidal Ito (stellate) cells around central veins, laying down collagenous bridges linking adjacent central veins ('reverse lobulation' or cardiac fibrosis).

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: The gross necropsy appearance of a 'sugar-coated liver' (Zuckergussleber / Glissonian cirrhosis), in which the liver capsule is encased by a thick, white, hyaline cartilaginous-like fibrous plaque, is a sequela of:
options: Diffuse sinusoidal AA amyloidosis in Oriental Shorthair cats
Centrilobular fatty degeneration in pregnant twin-bearing ewes
Acute ascending suppurative cholangiohepatitis from salmonellosis
explanation: Glissonian cirrhosis (perihepatitis chronica hyperplastica) is not a true parenchymal cirrhosis; organization of chronic fibrinous peritoneal/capsular exudate transforms Glisson's capsule into a thick, porcelain-white hyalinized fibrous rind resembling sugar icing.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Segmental brownish-yellow pitting and chalky thinning of dental enamel ('enamel hypoplasia') in the permanent dentition of a 1-year-old dog is a permanent pathological sequela of:
options: Congenital erythropoietic porphyria depositing uroporphyrin in dentin
Excessive dietary Vitamin D3 supplementation after 8 months of age
Chronic renal secondary hyperparathyroidism after growth plate closure
Canine Distemper Virus infection destroying ameloblasts
explanation: Epitheliotropic Canine Distemper Virus (or high fever/tetracycline/fluorosis) during the 2- to 5-month postnatal window infects and destroys inner enamel epithelial ameloblasts prior to tooth eruption, leaving permanent segmental enamel defects.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In Gastric Dilatation-Volvulus (GDV) in deep-chested large-breed dogs (such as Great Danes), when viewed ventrodorsally at necropsy, the dilated stomach typically rotates in which direction around the distal esophagus?
options: Dorsoventrally 180 degrees through the epiploic foramen of Winslow
Clockwise 180 to 360 degrees, pulling spleen to right ventral abdomen
Longitudinally along the greater curvature without displacing the pylorus
Counter-clockwise 90 degrees, displacing the spleen into the pelvic canal
explanation: In canine GDV, the gas-distended stomach rotates clockwise (viewed from behind/ventrally) 180° to 360° around the gastroesophageal axis; the pylorus moves from right to left dorsally while the spleen is dragged via the gastrosplenic ligament to the right ventral aspect, compressing the portal vein and caudal vena cava.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In horses suffering from severe Equine Asthma ('Heaves' / Recurrent Airway Obstruction) induced by dusty mouldy hay, the characteristic microscopic lesion in terminal bronchioles is:
options: Goblet cell metaplasia and bronchiolar mucus plugs
Complete replacement of bronchiolar epithelium by ciliated columnar syncytia
Fibrinoid necrosis of bronchial cartilage rings with calcified sulfur granules
Diffuse alveolar flooding with heart failure hemosiderophages
explanation: Equine Recurrent Airway Obstruction ('Heaves') is a chronic bronchiolitis-emphysema complex where Clara (club) cells in terminal bronchioles undergo goblet cell metaplasia, plugging small airways with inspissated mucus spirals (Curschmann's spirals), peribronchiolar smooth muscle hypertrophy, and secondary alveolar hyperinflation/emphysema.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Ovine Pulmonary Adenocarcinoma ('Jaagsiekte'), a contagious lung cancer of sheep in which holding the sheep's hindquarters up ('wheelbarrow test') causes copious clear frothy fluid to pour from the nostrils, is caused by a Betaretrovirus that transforms:
options: Ciliated pseudostratified tracheal columnar epithelial cells
Pleural mesothelial cells and mediastinal lymphoblasts
Pulmonary intravascular macrophages and bronchial chondrocytes
explanation: Jaagsiekte Sheep Retrovirus (JSRV) selectively transforms secretory Type II alveolar epithelial cells and Clara (club) bronchiolar cells into papillary and acinar adenocarcinomas that secrete abundant surfactant-rich fluid into the airways.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Mönckeberg's medial calcific sclerosis—an incidental age-related vascular lesion seen in horses, cattle, and dogs—is histologically defined by:
options: Hyaline thickening of afferent renal arterioles in malignant hypertension
Necrotizing leukocytoclastic inflammation of post-capillary venules
Concentric ring-like dystrophic calcification of muscular tunica media without luminal narrowing
Subintimal cholesterol clefts and foam cell atheromas occluding the coronary lumen
explanation: Mönckeberg's medial sclerosis involves ring-like mineralization (and occasionally osseous metaplasia) restricted strictly to the smooth muscle tunica media of medium-sized muscular arteries; the intima is spared and the vessel lumen remains patent.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Unlike dogs and pigs (in which vegetative valvular endocarditis most frequently affects the mitral and aortic valves on the left side of the heart), in adult cattle vegetative endocarditis most commonly involves the:
options: Left atrioventricular (mitral) valve caused by Listeria monocytogenes
Right atrioventricular valve caused by Trueperella pyogenes
Aortic semilunar valve caused by Bacillus anthracis
Pulmonic semilunar valve caused by Mannheimia haemolytica
explanation: In cattle, septic emboli arising from traumatic reticulitis, hepatic abscesses, mastitis, or metritis enter the systemic venous return to the right heart, lodging predominantly on the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) valve with Trueperella pyogenes as the primary isolate.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In dogs and mink infected with the giant kidney worm Dioctophyma renale (acquired by ingesting paratenic frogs or fish), the adult blood-red nematode almost exclusively invades and destroys the parenchyma of the:
options: Left kidney (due to larval penetration from the descending colon)
Bilateral renal medullae equally via the renal arteries
Urinary bladder trigone (due to ascending urethral migration)
explanation: Infective L3 larvae of Dioctophyma renale excyst in the duodenum and penetrate directly through the duodenal wall into the adjacent right kidney (in >85% of cases), digesting the entire renal parenchyma until only a bony/fibrous capsule containing the worm and hemorrhagic pus remains.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In swine, perirenal and periureteral cysts communicating with the ureteral lumen alongside extensive fibrotic migration tracts and portal phlebitis in the liver are caused by the swine kidney worm:
explanation: Stephanurus dentatus larvae migrate for months through the porcine liver and portal veins (causing severe cirrhotic scarring and portal thrombosis) before emerging into the perirenal fat to form cysts that open into the renal pelvis or ureter.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Enzootic Posthitis ('Pizzle Rot' or 'Sheath Rot')—characterized by severe scabbing and necrotic ulceration of the preputial orifice in castrated male sheep (wethers) and rams fed high-protein legume pastures—is caused by:
explanation: High-protein diets increase urinary urea excretion; diphtheroid bacteria of the Corynebacterium renale group inhabiting preputial wool possess potent urease that hydrolyzes urea into caustic ammonia, causing coagulation necrosis and ulceration of the preputial skin and mucosa.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In sheep and goats suffering from 'Gid' (Sturdy), unilateral space-occupying cysts in the cerebral hemisphere that cause pressure atrophy and palpable thinning/perforation of the overlying cranial bones are the larval stage (Coenurus cerebralis) of:
explanation: Coenurus cerebralis is the fluid-filled bladderworm metacestode of the canine tapeworm Taenia multiceps; its slow expansion in the ovine brain causes cortical pressure atrophy, contralateral visual deficits, circling toward the cyst side, and pressure rarefaction of the skull calvarium.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: Non-neoplastic nests of hyperplastic endometrial glands and stroma displaced deeply between bundles of the myometrial smooth muscle wall (observed in bitches, queens, and cows) are pathologically termed:
explanation: Adenomyosis is the benign presence of islands of endometrial glands and stroma deep within the myometrium due to downward hyperplastic growth; true endometriosis (ectopic endometrium on peritoneal surfaces) occurs only in menstruating primates.

topic: Systemic Pathology (Digestive, Respiratory, Cardiovascular, Urinary, Nervous & Reproductive)
questionText: In sheep and goats, 'Muellerius capillaris' (the nodular lungworm acquired by ingesting infected land snails or slugs) produces pathognomonic subpleural pulmonary nodules located predominantly in the:
options: Cranioventral (apical and cardiac) lung lobes, appearing as diffuse dark-red consolidated hepatization
Dorsocaudal lung lobes, appearing as 2 to 5 mm greenish-grey calcified 'lead-shot' nodules
Visceral pericardium and mediastinal lymph nodes, appearing as caseous onion-ring abscesses
Mainstem tracheal bifurcation, appearing as large pedunculated blood-filled polyps
explanation: Unlike Dictyocaulus filaria (which inhabits the lumen of bronchi), Muellerius capillaris adults live inside the alveolar parenchyma and subpleural tissue of the dorsocaudal lung lobes in sheep and goats, inducing firm, gritty, greenish-grey subpleural granulomas ('lead-shot nodules').

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In horses and sheep suffering from Borna Disease (an orthobornavirus non-suppurative encephalomyelitis), the pathognomonic eosinophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies found in hippocampal and cortical neurons are termed:
explanation: Joest-Degen bodies are round or oval acidophilic intranuclear (and occasionally cytoplasmic) inclusion bodies surrounded by a clear halo within large neurons of Ammon's horn (hippocampus) and cerebral cortex in Borna disease.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In Canine Distemper Virus (CDV) infection, eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies observed specifically inside circulating erythrocytes, leukocytes, and bronchial/urothelial epithelial cells are known as:
explanation: Lentz bodies are the diagnostic eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies of Canine Distemper Virus found in epithelial cells (urinary bladder transitional epithelium, bronchial mucosa, footpad epidermis) and peripheral blood cells.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In acute Rift Valley Fever (and Yellow Fever) hepatitis, alongside apoptotic Councilman bodies, degenerating hepatocytes contain characteristic eosinophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies termed:
explanation: Torres bodies are irregular, eosinophilic, filament-like or granular intranuclear viral inclusions observed in hepatocytes during acute Rift Valley Fever and Yellow Fever infections.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: Large, eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies (Type A poxviral inclusions) observed inside ballooned epidermal keratinocytes in Cowpox and Vaccinia virus infections are classically named:
explanation: Guarnieri bodies are acidophilic intracytoplasmic viral factories (Type A inclusions) found in prickle cells of the stratum spinosum in Cowpox, Vaccinia, and Variola infections (analogous to Bollinger bodies in Fowlpox).

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: Unlike Cowdry Type A intranuclear inclusions (which are large, solitary, and cause prominent margination of chromatin), Cowdry Type B intranuclear inclusions are characterized histologically as:
options: Giant basophilic intracytoplasmic grape-like clusters inside splenic macrophages
Acid-fast magenta granules located inside the mitochondrial matrix of hepatocytes
Birefringent crystalline rods restricted exclusively to cerebellar Purkinje dendrites
explanation: Cowdry Type B inclusions (seen in Poliovirus and early Adenovirus stages) are smaller, often multiple, poorly demarcated droplet-like intranuclear bodies that do not push host chromatin onto the nuclear membrane.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In piglets under 3 weeks of age suffering from 'Inclusion Body Rhinitis' (Porcine Cytomegalovirus / Suid betaherpesvirus 2), histopathological examination of the nasal mucosa reveals:
options: Complete atrophy of ventral turbinate cartilage without any viral inclusion bodies
Granulomatous nodules containing acid-fast bacilli and Langhans giant cells
Syncytial giant cells with eosinophilic intracytoplasmic bodies in squamous epithelium
explanation: Porcine Cytomegalovirus (PCMV) selectively infects the mucous and serous tubuloalveolar glands of the nasal turbinates, causing extreme cellular and nuclear enlargement (cytomegaly) with giant basophilic intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a halo.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In rabid animals, focal nodular collections of proliferating rod-shaped microglial cells that replace degenerated and phagocytosed neurons in the brainstem and spinal cord are termed:
explanation: Babes' nodules are focal glial nodules composed of activated microglial cells accumulating around degenerating neurons (neuronophagia) in the brainstem, hippocampus, and spinal cord during Rabies and other viral encephalitides.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: When a suspect rabid dog or horse is euthanized early in the clinical course and Negri bodies cannot yet be found in the hippocampus or cerebellum, which structure provides a classic histological back-up lesion of nonsuppurative ganglionitis?
explanation: In rabies, perivascular mononuclear cuffing, neuronal degeneration, and proliferation of satellite capsule cells (ganglionitis) in the trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion and nodose ganglion of the vagus nerve are highly reliable histological indicators.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: For statutory post-mortem confirmation of Scrapie in sheep and Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) in cattle, the mandatory neuroanatomical target site sampled at the foramen magnum is the:
options: Rostral olfactory bulb and piriform lobe of the cerebral cortex
Pineal gland and rostral colliculi of the mesencephalon
Caudal equina and lumbosacral intumescence of the spinal cord
Medulla oblongata at the level of the obex
explanation: The obex region of the caudal medulla oblongata—specifically containing the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus nerve (DMNV), solitary tract nucleus, and spinal tract nucleus of the trigeminal nerve—is the earliest and most consistent site of spongiform vacuolation and PrPSc accumulation.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In bovine tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium bovis, chronic spread across serous cavities produces multiple firm, greyish-white, grape-like or sessile calcified nodules on the pleura and peritoneum classically known as:
explanation: 'Pearl disease' (Perlsucht or 'grapes') refers to tuberculous pleuritis and peritonitis in cattle, where firm, glistening, pedunculated or sessile granulomas stud the serosal surfaces like strings of pearls.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: How do tuberculous granulomas in horses and dogs differ grossly and histologically from classic bovine tubercles?
options: Equine and canine tubercles are restricted exclusively to the hooves and nasal cartilage
Equine and canine tubercles are proliferative, grey-white, lardaceous
Equine and canine tubercles undergo immediate liquefaction into green foul-smelling pus
Equine and canine tubercles consist purely of cholesterol crystals without macrophages
explanation: In horses and carnivores (dogs), tuberculosis produces exuberant proliferative granulation tissue rich in epithelioid cells and fibroblasts with very little central caseous necrosis or mineralization, closely mimicking malignant neoplasms (sarcomas or lymphomas) at necropsy.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: Unlike cattle with Johne's disease (where lesions are non-caseating and white-grey), sheep infected with pigmented ovine (Type I/S) strains of Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis frequently exhibit:
options: Fibrinous pleuropneumonia with interlobular septal marbling
Massive splenomegaly with dark unclotted tarry blood
Bright yellow-to-orange pigmentation of thickened ileal mucosa
Deep button-like hemorrhagic ulcers in the abomasum and duodenum
explanation: Pigmented ovine strains of MAP produce a carotenoid-like pigment that imparts a striking chrome-yellow to orange discoloration to the thickened jejunal/ileal mucosa in sheep, and ovine paratuberculous lymph nodes may show focal caseation and mineralization.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In adult sheep grazing Romney Marsh pastures, 'Struck'—characterized by sudden death, acute necrotic enteritis, ulceration of the small intestine, and abundant straw-colored peritoneal and thoracic transudates—is caused by:
explanation: 'Struck' is an acute enterotoxemia of adult sheep caused by beta-toxin of Clostridium perfringens Type C, producing hemorrhagic/necrotic jejunitis, transudation into body cavities, and subendocardial hemorrhages often mistaken for lightning strike.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In neonatal lambs under 2 weeks of age, 'Lamb Dysentery'—characterized by acute fatal hemorrhagic enteritis with extensive coalescing necrotic ulcers throughout the ileum—is caused by:
explanation: Clostridium perfringens Type B elaborates both trypsin-sensitive beta-toxin (which thrives in neonates due to colostral trypsin inhibitors) and epsilon-toxin, causing fulminant hemorrhagic and ulcerative enteritis in lambs during the first 1–2 weeks of life.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In cattle, 'Bacillary Hemoglobinuria' ('Red Water Disease')—characterized at necropsy by port-wine colored urine, generalized icterus, and a single large, pale, ischemic coagulative infarct in the liver—is caused by:
explanation: Clostridium haemolyticum (C. novyi Type D) spores germinate in fluke-damaged liver parenchyma and secrete massive amounts of beta-toxin (phospholipase C / lecithinase), causing thrombosis of a portal vein branch (a single huge pale hepatic infarct surrounded by a red hyperemic rim) and massive intravascular hemolysis.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In young rams, 'Bighead'—characterized by massive, non-gaseous, golden-yellow gelatinous edema of the subcutaneous tissues of the head, face, and neck following head-butting fights—is caused by:
explanation: Fighting wounds on the poll of young rams become infected with Clostridium novyi Type A (and C. sordellii); its alpha-toxin causes intense capillary permeability without myonecrosis or gas, producing clear-to-yellow gelatinous swelling of the head and neck ('Bighead').

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In young foals aged 1 to 6 weeks, 'Tyzzer's Disease'—characterized by acute fatal icterus, multifocal pale miliary hepatic necrosis, and bundles of intracellular filamentous bacteria arranged like 'pick-up-sticks' on Warthin-Starry silver stain—is caused by:
explanation: Clostridium piliforme is an obligate intracellular, spore-forming filamentous bacterium that causes acute multifocal coagulative hepatic necrosis in foals, rodents, and rabbits; diagnostic silver stains reveal criss-crossing bundles of bacilli inside viable hepatocytes at the necrotic margin.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: Unlike cattle and sheep (which develop peracute septicemia and massive splenomegaly), pigs and dogs that ingest Bacillus anthracis spores typically develop which localized clinicopathological form of Anthrax?
options: Laminar cerebrocortical necrosis with cerebellar herniation
Chronic vegetative endocarditis of the left mitral valve with diamond skin plaques
Diffuse caseous pneumonia with calcified pleural pearls
Pharyngeal and cervical anthrax with severe hemorrhagic gelatinous edema of throat and necrotizing tonsillitis
explanation: Swine and carnivores are relatively resistant to anthrax; pharyngeal/tonsillar invasion by B. anthracis produces severe local necrotizing tonsillitis, hemorrhagic/brick-red cervical lymphadenitis, and massive gelatinous edema of the neck that causes death by asphyxiation.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In the laboratory diagnosis of Anthrax from decomposed hides or putrefied spleen where bacilli have lysed, which classical thermoprecipitation ring test uses boiled tissue extract layered over hyperimmune serum?
explanation: Ascoli's thermoprecipitation test detects heat-stable capsular/somatic polysaccharide antigens (precipitinogens) of Bacillus anthracis extracted by boiling tissue in acidified saline; a sharp white precipitin ring at the serum interface confirms anthrax.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: Why does Brucella abortus exhibit a striking tropism for the bovine pregnant placenta, fetal fluids, and bull seminal vesicles and epididymides?
options: These tissues secrete high concentrations of hyaluronic acid and lysozyme
These tissues synthesize high concentrations of four-carbon sugar alcohol D-erythritol
These tissues maintain a core temperature 4 degrees below body temperature
These tissues lack complement C3 and tissue macrophages
explanation: Bovine erythrophilic trophoblasts and male accessory sex glands produce abundant D-erythritol, which Brucella abortus (except the attenuated S19 vaccine strain) preferentially utilizes over glucose as a carbon and energy source to drive rapid intracellular replication.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In calves dying of subacute septicemic Salmonellosis (Salmonella enterica serovar Dublin) and piglets with Salmonella Choleraesuis, miliary pale-yellowish microgranulomas and focal coagulative necroses scattered in the liver parenchyma are termed:
explanation: Paratyphoid nodules are characteristic microscopic lesions of systemic salmonellosis in calves and pigs, consisting of focal hepatocyte coagulative necrosis replaced by aggregates of Kupffer cells, macrophages (histiocytes), and fibrin thrombi in sinusoids.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In grower-finisher pigs, 'Porcine Proliferative Enteropathy' ('Garden-hose gut' / proliferative ileitis)—characterized by massive adenomatous thickening of the ileal mucosa without ulceration in early stages—is caused by:
explanation: Lawsonia intracellularis is an obligate intracellular curved Gram-negative rod that resides freely in the apical cytoplasm of immature ileal crypt enterocytes (demonstrated with Warthin-Starry silver stain), stimulating unrestrained crypt cell mitosis and preventing goblet cell differentiation.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: How is 'Swine Dysentery' (caused by the strongly beta-hemolytic spirochete Brachyspira hyodysenteriae) anatomically differentiated at necropsy from Porcine Proliferative Enteropathy and Salmonellosis?
options: Swine dysentery lesions are restricted exclusively to the stomach and duodenum
Swine dysentery lesions of mucohemorrhagic diphtheritic inflammation are confined strictly to large intestine
Swine dysentery produces marginal wedge-shaped infarcts in the spleen and kidneys
Swine dysentery causes symmetrical encephalomalacia of the brainstem alongside polyarthritis
explanation: Brachyspira hyodysenteriae proliferates strictly in the goblet-cell-rich crypts of the cecum and spiral colon, producing superficial mucosal necrosis, mucus hypersecretion, and hemorrhage confined to the large bowel while completely sparing the small intestine.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In rapidly growing piglets 1 to 2 weeks after weaning, 'Edema Disease' ('Gut Edema')—characterized by clear gelatinous edema of the gastric cardiac submucosa, mesocolon, and eyelids alongside fibrinoid necrosis of brainstem arterioles—is caused by:
explanation: Edema disease is an enterotoxemia caused by hemolytic F18-fimbriated Escherichia coli colonizing the small intestine and secreting Shiga toxin 2e (Stx2e), which enters the bloodstream and binds globotetraosylceramide (Gb4) receptors on vascular endothelial cells, causing fibrinoid angionecrosis (cerebrospinal angiopathy) and severe submucosal edema.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In feedlot cattle, 'Thrombotic Meningoencephalitis' (TME / 'Sleeper Syndrome')—characterized at necropsy by multifocal, randomly distributed, dark-red hemorrhagic infarcts and septic thrombi throughout the brain and spinal cord—is caused by:
explanation: Histophilus somni adheres to and induces apoptosis of microvascular endothelial cells in the bovine brain, retina, myocardium, and joints, triggering septic vasculitis, thrombosis, and multifocal hemorrhagic cerebrocortical and brainstem infarcts.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In young pigs aged 4 to 8 weeks, 'Glässer's Disease'—characterized by acute fibrinous polyserositis, pleuritis, pericarditis, peritonitis, synovitis, and purulent leptomeningitis—is caused by:
explanation: Glaesserella parasuis (an NAD-dependent V-factor-requiring Gram-negative rod) invades the bloodstream of stressed weaned pigs, producing classic fibrinous polyserositis, polyarthritis, and fibrinopurulent meningitis ('Glässer's disease').

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In cattle recovering from acute Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD), the chronic endocrine sequela known as 'Panting Syndrome' (heat intolerance, hirsutism with long shaggy hair coat, and agalactia) results from viral necrosis of the:
explanation: Aphthovirus can localize in and cause focal necrosis and fibrosis of the adenohypophysis (anterior pituitary) and hypothalamic-thyroid endocrine axis in recovered cattle, impairing thermoregulation and hair shedding ('panting cattle').

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: Histopathologically, Peste des Petits Ruminants (PPR / Small Ruminant Morbillivirus) is differentiated from Bluetongue and FMD in goats and sheep by the presence in oral/intestinal epithelium and alveolar macrophages of:
options: Spongiform vacuolation of brainstem neurons without giant cells
Brick-shaped Bollinger bodies restricted to dermal keratinocytes
Basophilic intranuclear inclusion bodies only in crypt enterocytes
Multinucleated syncytial giant cells containing both intracytoplasmic and intranuclear eosinophilic inclusion bodies
explanation: Like Canine Distemper and Rinderpest morbilliviruses, PPR virus induces prominent epithelial and alveolar macrophage syncytia (giant cells) containing eosinophilic inclusion bodies in both the nucleus and cytoplasm.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In sheep and white-tailed deer dying of Bluetongue (Orbivirus), which vascular and cardiac lesion is considered pathognomonic at necropsy alongside cyanotic glossitis and coronitis?
options: Concentric hypertrophy of the right ventricle with saddle thrombosis
Cauliflower-like vegetative endocarditis on the right tricuspid valve
Diffuse calcification of the abdominal aorta and intercostal pleura
explanation: Focal intramural hemorrhage in the tunica media at the base of the pulmonary artery (and aorta) together with ischemic coagulative necrosis of the papillary muscle of the left ventricle is virtually pathognomonic for Bluetongue (and Epizootic Hemorrhagic Disease).

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: Transplacental infection of a seronegative pregnant cow with Non-Cytopathic Bovine Viral Diarrhea Virus (BVDV) between 90 and 150 days of gestation causes which classic congenital teratogenic triad in the calf?
options: Arthrogryposis, torticollis, and cleft palate only
explanation: Between 90 and 150 days of bovine gestation, the fetal cerebellum and retina are undergoing rapid mitosis and migration; BVDV destroys the external germinal layer of the cerebellum and induces necrotizing vasculitis, resulting in cerebellar hypoplasia, cavitation (porencephaly/hydranencephaly), and microphthalmia/cataracts.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In neonatal lambs and calves under 2 weeks of age, Rift Valley Fever (Phlebovirus) causes 90–100% mortality with a pathognomonic necropsy lesion of:
options: Corrugated thickening of the ileal mucosa and mesenteric lymph nodes
Ulcerative stomatitis with zebra striping in the large colon
Chronic proliferative arthritis and interstitial pneumonia
Fulminant diffuse hepatic necrosis with bright yellow-to-orange friable liver
explanation: Rift Valley Fever virus is intensely hepatotropic in neonatal ruminants, causing pan-lobular coagulative and lytic necrosis of >90% of hepatocytes, turning the enlarged liver bright yellow-orange or mottled red with subcapsular hemorrhages.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In cattle affected by Lumpy Skin Disease (Capripoxvirus), firm, circumscribed, flat-topped intracutaneous nodules (1 to 5 cm) undergo central ischemic necrosis via dermal vasculitis, forming a deep necrotic core that sloughs out, known as a:
explanation: Lumpy Skin Disease virus causes necrotizing vasculitis and thrombosis of dermal and subcutaneous arterioles, producing full-thickness circular infarction of skin nodules; the dry necrotic plug ('sit-fast') eventually separates, leaving a deep star-shaped scar.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In Sheeppox (Capripoxvirus), histopathological examination of cutaneous papules and pulmonary nodules reveals pathognomonic large, vacuolated histiocytic and mesenchymal dermal cells with marginated chromatin and eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions, termed:
explanation: 'Sheeppox cells' (cellules claveleuses) are characteristic hypertrophied, vacuolated dermal cells (modified macrophages/fibroblasts and keratinocytes) with vacuolated nuclei and prominent eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In horses with African Horse Sickness (Orbivirus), the subacute cardiac form ('Dikkop') is distinguished clinically and at necropsy from the peracute pulmonary form ('Dunkop') by:
options: Necrotizing ulcerative enterocolitis with button ulcers in the cecum
Massive frothy fluid pouring from the nostrils with normal subcutaneous tissues
Calcified granulomas along the facial lymphatic vessels
Prominent gelatinous subcutaneous edema of the supraorbital fossae and eyelids
explanation: In African Horse Sickness, 'Dunkop' (thin head) is the peracute pulmonary form (severe alveolar edema and hydrothorax), whereas 'Dikkop' (thick head) is the subacute cardiac form characterized by bulging edematous supraorbital fossae (unique to equids), yellow gelatinous subcutaneous edema of the head/neck, hydropericardium, and left ventricular epicardial/endocardial ecchymoses.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In pigs aged 6 to 14 weeks suffering from Postweaning Multisystemic Wasting Syndrome (PMWS) caused by Porcine Circovirus Type 2 (PCV-2), the pathognomonic microscopic finding in depleted lymphoid follicles is:
options: Eosinophilic intranuclear Cowdry Type A inclusions in T-lymphoblasts cells
Concentric onion-ring caseation necrosis surrounded by neutrophils cells
Granulomatous histiocytic replacement and multinucleated giant cells
Diffuse deposition of Congo red-positive amyloid in Malpighian corpuscles cells
explanation: PCV-2 destroys B-cell follicles in lymph nodes, tonsils, and Peyer's patches, replacing them with sheets of epithelioid macrophages and syncytial giant cells containing characteristic multiple, round, densely basophilic 'botryoid' (grape-cluster) intracytoplasmic viral inclusions.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In cattle, sheep, dogs, and cats (non-natural dead-end hosts) infected with Suid alphaherpesvirus 1 (Pseudorabies / Aujeszky's disease), the hallmark clinical and pathological presentation is:
options: Ferocious localized neuropathic pruritus and self-mutilation
Mild self-limiting rhinitis without neurological involvement
Chronic progressive weight loss with corrugated ileal enteritis
Generalized cutaneous papillomatosis and corneal opacity
explanation: In non-porcine species, Pseudorabies virus ascends peripheral sensory nerves from the portal of entry to the dorsal root or trigeminal ganglia, causing acute necrotizing ganglioneuritis that triggers relentless self-mutilating pruritus ('mad itch') followed rapidly by fatal nonsuppurative encephalomyelitis.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP), caused by a virulent macrophage-tropic biotype of Feline Coronavirus, produces its characteristic effusive ('wet') and non-effusive ('dry') lesions through which immunopathological mechanism?
options: Secretion of a botulinum-like neurotoxin blocking neuromuscular junctions
Direct viral lysis of mature erythrocytes and megakaryocytes in bone marrow
Type I IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in the hepatic vein sphincters
explanation: Non-neutralizing anti-spike antibodies enhance viral uptake into monocytes/macrophages (antibody-dependent enhancement); virus-laden macrophages adhere to small venules and deposit immune complexes, triggering intense complement-mediated pyogranulomatous phlebitis and high-protein fibrinous effusion.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In horses and cattle in India, 'Rhinosporidiosis'—characterized by friable, pinkish-red, sessile or pedunculated polypoid growths ('strawberry polyps') on the nasal mucosa studded with tiny white pinhead dots—is caused by:
explanation: Rhinosporidium seeberi (an aquatic mesomycetozoean protist) produces vascular nasal polyps; the tiny white surface dots seen grossly are giant thick-walled mature sporangia (100–350 µm) filled with thousands of endospores that rupture through an apical pore.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In cats and dogs with nasal and central nervous system Cryptococcosis (Cryptococcus neoformans), brain sections often display gelatinous 'soap-bubble' pseudocysts with minimal leukocytic inflammation because:
options: The wide polyanionic mucopolysaccharide capsule masks cell wall antigens
The organism resides exclusively inside the axoplasm of myelinated nerves
The yeast calcifies immediately into concentric psammoma bodies
The fungus produces a potent leukotoxin that lyses all surrounding astrocytes
explanation: Cryptococcus neoformans possesses a thick glucuronoxylomannan polysaccharide capsule that blocks complement opsonization and macrophage phagocytosis; in H&E sections it appears as a wide clear halo around narrow-necked budding yeasts, which stains carmine-red with Mayer's mucicarmine.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In dogs with disseminated Histoplasmosis (Histoplasma capsulatum), severe chronic protein-losing enterocolitis, hepatosplenomegaly, and icterus are histologically characterized by lamina propria and sinusoids distended with:
options: Large thick-walled spherules filled with endospores and surrounded by neutrophils
Macrophages packed with numerous tiny intracellular oval yeast bodies surrounded by shrinkage halo
Extracellular club-shaped Splendore-Hoeppli rosettes around Gram-positive rods
Broad, ribbon-like, non-septate hyphae invading blood vessel walls
explanation: Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that replicates exclusively as tiny (2–4 µm) budding yeasts inside the phagolysosomes of macrophages (Kupffer cells, intestinal lamina propria macrophages), closely resembling Leishmania amastigotes except Histoplasma lacks a kinetoplast and is PAS/GMS positive.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In horses and cats with cutaneous-lymphatic Sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii), pyogranulomatous nodules ulcerating along subcutaneous lymphatic vessels contain characteristic pleomorphic yeast cells described morphologically as:
explanation: In host tissues at 37°C, the dimorphic fungus Sporothrix schenckii converts into characteristic elongated, fusiform, 'cigar-shaped' yeast bodies (2–6 µm) within macrophages and giant cells.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In cattle suffering from East Coast Fever (caused by Theileria parva and transmitted by Rhipicephalus appendiculatus) or Tropical Theileriosis (Theileria annulata), the pathognomonic lesion in the abomasal mucosa is:
options: Nodular cobblestone 'Morocco leather' hyperplasia of mucous neck cells
Large pedunculated papillomas at the omasal-abomasal orifice
Thick cerebriform corrugations that cannot be flattened by stretching
Multiple sharply demarcated 'punched-out' necrotic ulcers alongside Koch's blue bodies in lymphoblasts
explanation: Theileria sporozoites transform bovine lymphocytes into proliferating lymphoblasts containing multinucleated macroschizonts ('Koch's blue bodies' on Giemsa stain); infiltration and vascular occlusion in the abomasal lamina propria produce pathognomonic punched-out crateriform abomasal ulcers.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In ovine abortion caused by Toxoplasma gondii, the pathognomonic macroscopic placental lesion that differentiates toxoplasmosis from Chlamydia abortus and Brucella ovis is:
options: Multifocal 1 to 3 mm chalky-white foci of coagulative necrosis
Complete black putrefaction and emphysema of both the fetus and chorioallantois necrosis
Diffuse leathery thickening and purulent exudate restricted to the intercotyledonary membrane necrosis
Cup-shaped ringworm-like necrosis of the caruncular margins necrosis
explanation: Toxoplasma gondii causes multifocal pinpoint white necrotic and mineralized foci (1–3 mm) confined strictly within the cotyledonary villi ('strawberry' or 'white-spotted' cotyledons), while the intercotyledonary chorioallantois remains clear and uninflamed (unlike Chlamydia or Brucella).

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In dogs with chronic Visceral Leishmaniasis (Leishmania infantum), how are the intracellular protozoal amastigotes inside macrophages definitively distinguished from Histoplasma capsulatum on Giemsa-stained smears?
options: Leishmania amastigotes divide by broad-based budding and form pseudohyphae
Leishmania amastigotes possess distinct rod-shaped paranuclear mitochondrial DNA structure alongside round nucleus
Leishmania amastigotes measure over 50 µm and contain endospores
Leishmania amastigotes stain bright magenta with Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)
explanation: On Romanowsky (Giemsa/Wright) smears, Leishmania amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies, 2–4 µm) display a spherical trophonucleus AND a dense, dark-staining rod-shaped kinetoplast (and are PAS/GMS negative), whereas Histoplasma yeasts lack a kinetoplast and are strongly PAS/GMS positive.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In cattle affected by Bovine Besnoitiosis (Besnoitia besnoiti)—which causes severe chronic scleroderma ('elephant skin disease'), alopecia, and bull sterility—a rapid clinical and post-mortem diagnosis is made by observing:
options: Large fluid-filled hydatid cysts in the hepatic and pulmonary parenchyma
Microfilariae swimming freely in aqueous humor of the anterior chamber
Ribbon-like tapeworm proglottids attached to the ileocecal valve
Pinhead-sized, glistening white thick-walled protozoal cysts
explanation: Besnoitia besnoiti forms macroscopic (0.5 mm), thick-walled, pearly-white tissue cysts inside dermal fibroblasts, dartos tunica, nasal mucosa, and the scleral conjunctiva ('scleral pearls'), which are pathognomonic on clinical or post-mortem inspection.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: When infective larvae of Trichinella spiralis invade striated skeletal muscle fibers (such as the diaphragmatic crura, tongue, and masseter), they do not lyse the myofiber but instead:
options: Multiply by binary fission inside the sarcoplasmic reticulum until the muscle ruptures
Calcify immediately into dead gritty rice-grain cysticerci within 48 hours
Reprogram myofiber into basophilic, angiogenic 'nurse cell' surrounded by hyalinized collagenous capsule
Migrate out of the muscle within 5 days to encyst in the renal cortex
explanation: Trichinella spiralis L1 larvae penetrate skeletal myofibers and induce loss of cross-striations, enlargement of sarcoplasmic nuclei, basophilia of the sarcoplasm, and a surrounding vascular rete (via VEGF induction), transforming the host muscle cell into a protective 'nurse cell'.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
