questionText: In horses, 'Equine Viral Arteritis' (caused by Alphaarterivirus equid) produces palpebral edema, dependent limb/scrotal edema, and abortion through a characteristic microscopic vascular lesion of:
options: Necrotizing pan-vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis of muscular tunica media of small arteries
Subintimal cholesterol foam-cell plaque formation in the coronary arteries
Medial hypertrophy and muscularization of pulmonary alveolar arterioles arteries
Granulomatous endarteritis obliterans of the cranial mesenteric artery arteries
explanation: Equine Viral Arteritis virus replicates in macrophages and vascular endothelial and smooth muscle cells, producing severe fibrinoid necrosis of the tunica media of small muscular arteries (pan-arteritis) and perivascular edema.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome (PRRS / 'Blue Ear Disease'), the virus impairs pulmonary innate immunity and causes interstitial pneumonia by selectively infecting and inducing apoptosis in:
explanation: PRRS virus enters differentiated porcine pulmonary alveolar macrophages (and intravascular macrophages) via the scavenger receptor CD163 (and sialoadhesin CD169), destroying up to 40% of alveolar macrophages and predisposing pigs to secondary bacterial bronchopneumonia.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In dogs and cats, infection with the protozoan Hepatozoon americanum (transmitted by ingesting Amblyomma maculatum ticks) produces severe debilitating myositis and periosteal bone proliferation with a pathognomonic muscle biopsy lesion termed:
options: Fusiform Miescher's tubules packed with bradyzoites without any inflammatory reaction
Coiled nurse-cell larvae surrounded by a calcified lemon-shaped capsule
Intranuclear schizonts dividing by merogony inside cardiac Purkinje fibers
'Onion-skin' mucopolysaccharide cysts containing central host macrophage surrounded by concentric lamellae
explanation: Hepatozoon americanum forms characteristic 'onion-skin' cysts (250–500 µm) in striated skeletal and cardiac muscle composed of a hypertrophied host macrophage harboring the parasite surrounded by concentric layers of pale-staining acid mucopolysaccharide.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In sheep and goats, 'Louping Ill' (a tick-borne Flavivirus encephalomyelitis transmitted by Ixodes ricinus) produces a characteristic cerebellar ataxia ('louping' or leaping gait) due to selective viral necrosis of:
options: Purkinje cells of the cerebellar cortex
Astrocytes in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra
Ependymal cells lining the lateral ventricles
explanation: Louping ill virus is strictly neurotropic in sheep, causing non-suppurative polioencephalomyelitis with selective degeneration, chromatolysis, and neuronophagia of cerebellar Purkinje cells and spinal motor neurons.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In cattle, 'Bovine Farcy'—a chronic pyogranulomatous lymphangitis and lymphadenitis of the superficial subcutaneous lymphatics of the limbs and prescapular/prefemoral nodes in tropical regions—is caused by:
explanation: Whereas Equine Farcy is caused by Burkholderia mallei (Glanders) or Histoplasma farciminosum (Epizootic lymphangitis), Bovine Farcy is a chronic acid-fast granulomatous lymphangitis caused by Mycobacterium farcinogenes and M. senegalense (formerly attributed to Nocardia farcinica).

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In horses, 'Epizootic Lymphangitis' (Pseudoglanders)—which mimics cutaneous Glanders (Farcy) by producing corded subcutaneous lymphatics and ulcerating nodules discharging thick creamy pus—is caused by the dimorphic fungus:
explanation: Histoplasma capsulatum var. farciminosum (formerly Cryptococcus farciminosus) causes Equine Epizootic Lymphangitis; Giemsa- or Gram-stained pus smears reveal characteristic oval, double-contoured 'lemon-shaped' or haloed yeast cells inside macrophages.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In chronic articular Swine Erysipelas (Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae), progressive ankylosing polyarthritis of the hock and carpal joints is driven histopathologically by:
options: Complete avascular osteonecrosis of the femoral head without synovitis
Villous hypertrophy of the synovial membrane
Direct deposition of chalky monosodium urate crystals across the synovial surface
Caseocalcareous necrosis of the subchondral growth plate with sulfur granules
explanation: Chronic Erysipelothrix arthritis is the classic veterinary model of rheumatoid-like arthritis: persistent bacterial antigens in the joint capsule drive lymphoplasmacytic synovitis, villous synovial hyperplasia, and fibrovascular pannus that bridges and destroys the articular cartilage.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In neonatal puppies under 3 weeks of age dying of 'Fading Puppy Syndrome' caused by Canine Herpesvirus-1 (CHV-1), the pathognomonic gross necropsy lesion in the kidneys is:
options: Single large wedge-shaped pale ischemic infarct at the cranial pole
Bilateral congenital polycystic kidneys with hydroureter
Diffuse cortical amyloidosis with papillary necrosis
Multifocal cortical petechial hemorrhages and pale necrotic foci
explanation: Canine Herpesvirus-1 replicates optimally at lower temperatures (35–36°C) in hypothermic neonates, causing systemic necrotizing vasculitis and multifocal hemorrhagic coagulative necrosis in the kidneys (classic 'cherry-spotted' or 'speckled' kidneys), liver, and lungs.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In mares and stallions recovering from Equine Coital Exanthema (caused by Equid alphaherpesvirus 3), healed pustules and ulcers on the pigmented skin of the vulva and penis leave permanent diagnostic:
options: Circular, sharply demarcated non-pigmented white spots
Star-shaped fibrotic scars with honey-like pus
explanation: Equid alphaherpesvirus 3 (EHV-3) is a venereally transmitted epitheliotropic herpesvirus; cytolytic destruction of basal melanocytes in the vulvar, perineal, and penile skin leaves permanent depigmented white macules (coital leukoderma).

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In cattle suffering from Bovine Ephemeral Fever ('Three-Day Sickness' caused by an arthropod-borne Ephemerovirus), the acute clinical recumbency, muscle tremors, and paresis are directly associated with:
options: Ascending demyelination of the sciatic and radial nerves
Fulminant laminar necrosis of the cerebral cortex
explanation: Bovine Ephemeral Fever virus induces an acute cytokine storm (IFN-α, TNF-α, IL-1) that triggers serofibrinous synovitis, polyserositis, pulmonary emphysema, neutrophilia with a left shift, and a sharp drop in ionized serum calcium mimicking parturient paresis.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In sheep, goats, and pigs in tropical regions, 'Melioidosis' (Pseudoglanders)—characterized by multiple caseopurulent abscesses in the lungs, spleen, liver, and nasal mucosa—is caused by:
explanation: Burkholderia pseudomallei (formerly Pseudomonas pseudomallei) is a saprophytic soil/water rod showing bipolar 'safety-pin' staining that causes Melioidosis (Pseudoglanders), producing visceral and nasal abscesses closely resembling Glanders.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In histological sections of mycotic ruminitis or mycotic placentitis in cattle, Zygomycetes (Mucor, Rhizopus, and Lichtheimia/Absidia) are morphologically differentiated from Aspergillus fumigatus because Zygomycete hyphae are:
options: Dimorphic cigar-shaped yeasts restricted to the cytoplasm of Kupffer cells
Spherical yeast cells reproducing exclusively by narrow-necked blastoconidia
Narrow (2 to 4 µm), regularly septate, and branch dichotomously at acute 45-degree angles
explanation: Mucorales (Zygomycetes) form broad, irregular, collapsible ribbon-like coenocytic (non-septate or pauciseptate) hyphae that branch at right angles (90°) and aggressively invade arterial walls (angioinvasion), whereas Aspergillus forms narrow, uniform, septate hyphae branching dichotomously at 45° angles.

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: At meat inspection of pork vs beef carcasses for cysticercosis ('measly pork' vs 'measly beef'), the metacestode Cysticercus cellulosae (Taenia solium in pigs) is microscopically distinguished from Cysticercus bovis (Taenia saginata in cattle) because Cysticercus cellulosae possesses:
options: A solid parenchymatous body lacking a fluid-filled bladder cavity
An armed scolex bearing four suckers
Four muscular suckers without a rostellum or hooks (unarmed scolex)
Multiple invaginated scolices budding from a laminated germinal membrane
explanation: Cysticercus cellulosae (larva of Taenia solium in porcine heart, tongue, masseter, and brain) has an armed scolex with a rostellum and double crown of large and small hooks, whereas Cysticercus bovis (larva of Taenia saginata in cattle) is unarmed (four suckers, no rostellum, no hooks).

topic: Pathology of Infectious Diseases (Bacterial, Viral, Fungal & Parasitic)
questionText: In pigs dying of acute Classical Swine Fever or African Swine Fever, histopathological examination of the central nervous system consistently reveals:
options: Spongiform vacuolation restricted to the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
Suppurative microabscesses with Gram-positive rods in the pons
Intracytoplasmic eosinophilic Negri bodies in cerebellar Purkinje cells
explanation: Both Classical Swine Fever (Pestivirus) and African Swine Fever (Asfarvirus) infect vascular endothelial cells and macrophages in the CNS, producing severe diffuse non-suppurative meningoencephalomyelitis characterized by multilayered mononuclear perivascular cuffs and vascular endothelial hyperplasia/necrosis.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Activating internal tandem duplication mutations in Exon 11 of the c-kit (CD117) proto-oncogene—which encodes the stem cell factor receptor tyrosine kinase targeted by toceranib—drive the malignancy of which two canine neoplasms?
options: Cutaneous Mast Cell Tumors and Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors
Oral Amelanotic Melanomas and Cutaneous Histiocytomas
Transitional Cell Carcinomas and Perianal Gland Adenomas
explanation: The c-kit proto-oncogene encodes the KIT receptor tyrosine kinase (CD117), which is essential for mast cell and interstitial cell of Cajal survival; activating mutations in exon 11 occur in high-grade canine mast cell tumors and GISTs.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Point mutations in codons 12, 13, or 61 of the ras proto-oncogene family (H-ras, K-ras, N-ras) promote uncontrolled cellular proliferation because the mutant Ras protein:
options: Acts as a transcription factor that demethylates the Rb promoter
Directly degrades p53 inside the nuclear proteasome
Polymerizes into intermediate filaments that pull chromatids apart
Loses intrinsic GTPase activity and remains constitutively locked
explanation: Normal Ras is a small G-protein molecular switch that hydrolyzes GTP to inactive GDP with the help of GAPs (GTPase-activating proteins); oncogenic point mutations abolish GTPase activity, trapping Ras in its active GTP-bound state and continuously firing the MAPK/ERK cascade.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Overexpression and gene amplification of the erbB-2 (HER2/neu) proto-oncogene in aggressive canine and feline mammary adenocarcinomas accelerates tumor growth by encoding a:
options: Transmembrane epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase that signals without ligand
Nuclear zinc-finger transcription factor that blocks apoptosis
explanation: The erbB-2 (c-erbB-2 / HER2) oncogene encodes a transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase of the EGF receptor family; when overexpressed on mammary carcinoma cells, it constitutively homodimerizes and phosphorylates downstream mitogenic pathways.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Germline or somatic activating mutations in the ret proto-oncogene are specifically implicated in Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) syndromes involving Pheochromocytoma and which thyroid neoplasm in bulls and dogs?
explanation: The ret proto-oncogene encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase for glial-derived neurotrophic factor in neural crest derivatives; activating mutations drive calcitonin-secreting parafollicular C-cell (ultimobranchial) tumors and adrenal medullary pheochromocytomas.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Loss-of-function mutation or deletion of the PTEN (Phosphatase and Tensin Homolog) tumor suppressor gene in canine hemangiosarcoma, melanoma, and osteosarcoma promotes oncogenesis by failing to inhibit the:
options: Extrinsic Fas / FADD / Caspase-8 death receptor pathway
PI3K / AKT / mTOR cell survival and proliferation pathway
Adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) / Axin destruction complex
Transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) SMAD growth arrest pathway
explanation: PTEN is a lipid phosphatase that dephosphorylates PIP3 back to PIP2, serving as the primary brake on the oncogenic PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling cascade; loss of PTEN unleashes constitutive AKT survival signaling.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Germline mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 tumor suppressor genes predispose English Springer Spaniels and other dog breeds to mammary carcinoma because BRCA proteins are essential for:
options: Excision repair of ultraviolet-induced thymine dimers
Sequestration of E2F transcription factors at the G1/S checkpoint
Hydroxylation and proteasomal degradation of HIF-1-alpha
High-fidelity homologous recombination repair of double-stranded DNA breaks
explanation: BRCA1 and BRCA2 are caretaker tumor suppressor genes that assemble RAD51 complexes to repair double-stranded DNA breaks via error-free homologous recombination; their loss causes chromosomal instability.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Over 90% of malignant animal neoplasms achieve limitless replicative immortality (escaping replicative senescence and the Hayflick limit) by reactivating the enzyme:
explanation: Normal somatic cells lose 50–200 base pairs of telomeric TTAGGG repeats with each division until shortened telomeres trigger p53-mediated senescence; malignant cells reactivate telomerase (TERT) to continuously elongate telomeres.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: During the initial step of the metastatic cascade, carcinoma cells undergo Epithelial-to-Mesenchymal Transition (EMT) driven by Snail and Twist transcription factors, which is molecularly characterized by:
options: Functional loss of surface E-cadherin adhesion molecules with gain of vimentin
Overexpression of tight-junction claudins and occludins
Upregulation of desmoglein-1 and loss of matrix metalloproteinases
Switch from Type I collagen synthesis to Type IV collagen synthesis
explanation: E-cadherin is the calcium-dependent transmembrane glycoprotein that cements epithelial cells together at adherens junctions; downregulation/mutation of E-cadherin (the 'cadherin switch' to N-cadherin and vimentin) liberates carcinoma cells to invade stroma.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: To breach the epithelial and vascular basement membranes during local invasion and intravasation, malignant tumor cells secrete Type IV collagenases, which correspond specifically to:
explanation: Basement membranes are composed of a dense meshwork of Type IV collagen and laminin; malignant cells secrete gelatinases MMP-2 and MMP-9 to cleave Type IV collagen, creating physical defects for amoeboid migration.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In diagnostic veterinary immunohistochemistry, while carcinomas express Cytokeratin and sarcomas express Vimentin, which malignant neoplasm of serous body cavities uniquely co-expresses BOTH Cytokeratin and Vimentin?
explanation: Mesothelial cells lining the pleura, peritoneum, and pericardium are mesodermally derived epithelial-like cells; consequently, malignant mesotheliomas characteristically show strong dual immunopositivity for both Cytokeratin and Vimentin.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: When a canine oral malignant melanoma is completely amelanotic (lacking cytoplasmic melanin granules on H&E and Masson-Fontana stains), definitive immunohistochemical confirmation relies on the diagnostic cocktail of:
explanation: Amelanotic oral melanomas in dogs mimic poorly differentiated sarcomas; a diagnostic IHC panel combining Melan-A, PNL2, tyrosinase-related proteins (TRP-1/2), and S-100 provides >95% sensitivity and specificity for melanocytic origin.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Which immunohistochemical marker is the gold standard for confirming astrocytic differentiation in primary central nervous system neoplasms (astrocytomas and glioblastomas)?
explanation: Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP) is the Type III intermediate filament specific to astrocytes and ependymal cells in the CNS.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: To definitively distinguish a canine Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor (GIST, arising from interstitial cells of Cajal) from a true smooth-muscle intestinal Leiomyosarcoma, GISTs are immunohistochemically positive for:
explanation: Canine and equine GISTs originate from the pacemaker interstitial cells of Cajal in the myenteric plexus and strongly express CD117 (KIT) and DOG-1, whereas true leiomyosarcomas are negative for KIT/DOG-1 and strongly positive for Desmin and Smooth Muscle Actin (SMA).

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In canine cutaneous round-cell tumors, strong nuclear immunoreactivity for MUM-1 (Multiple Myeloma Oncogene-1 / IRF4) along with cytoplasmic immunoglobulin light chains specifically confirms a diagnosis of:
explanation: MUM-1 (IRF4) is a lymphocyte-specific transcription factor expressed in late B-cell differentiation and plasma cells; nuclear MUM-1 staining is the most sensitive and specific immunohistochemical marker for canine plasmacytomas.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Which specific apical membrane glycoprotein marker is used in veterinary immunohistochemistry to confirm that a metastatic carcinoma originated from the transitional epithelium (urothelium) of the urinary bladder?
explanation: Uroplakin-III is a transmembrane protein synthesized by superficial umbrella cells of the urinary tract transitional epithelium (urothelium) and serves as the specific diagnostic marker for canine transitional cell carcinoma.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In evaluating the mitotic growth fraction of a canine neoplasm by immunohistochemistry, the monoclonal antibody MIB-1 detects the nuclear protein Ki-67, which is expressed during:
options: Resting G0 phase of the cell cycle only cells
All active phases of cell cycle but is absent in resting G0 cells
explanation: Ki-67 is a non-histone nuclear protein present throughout all active phases of the cell cycle (G1, S, G2, and mitosis) and rapidly degraded upon entry into quiescence (G0), making the Ki-67 labeling index the gold-standard measure of a tumor's growth fraction.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In Indian Zebu cattle (especially aged castrated bullocks of the Kankrej, Gir, and Khillari breeds), 'Horn Cancer'—in which the horn core is replaced by cauliflower-like friable tumor masses and gelatinous mucin—is histologically a:
options: Chondrosarcoma arising from the frontal epiphyseal plate
Basal cell carcinoma without squamous differentiation
Malignant Osteosarcoma with mineralized osteoid spicules
Well-differentiated Squamous Cell Carcinoma with keratin pearls
explanation: Bovine horn cancer (seen in >90% castrated bullocks and ~10% cows, rarely in uncastrated bulls or buffaloes) arises from the mucous membrane of the horn core/frontal sinus via squamous metaplasia and transforms into a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma with prominent cell nests (epithelial pearls).

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In Scottish Terriers, Shetland Sheepdogs, and West Highland White Terriers, Transitional Cell Carcinoma (urothelial carcinoma) of the urinary bladder occurs predominantly at the bladder trigone and harbors a somatic point mutation (V595E) in which gene in >80% of cases?
explanation: Over 80% of canine urothelial (transitional cell) carcinomas and prostatic carcinomas carry an activating glutamic acid-for-valine substitution (V595E, homologous to human V600E) in the BRAF serine/threonine kinase gene, allowing highly sensitive PCR detection on free-catch urine.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Palpation or fine-needle aspiration of a canine cutaneous Mast Cell Tumor frequently triggers immediate localized erythema, edema, and wheal formation around the mass, a clinical phenomenon known as:
explanation: Darier's sign is the localized urticarial wheal-and-flare reaction elicited within minutes of physically manipulating a cutaneous mast cell tumor, caused by mechanical degranulation of vasoactive histamine, heparin, and leukotrienes.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: On plain radiographs of a canine appendicular Osteosarcoma, a triangular cuff of reactive subperiosteal new bone formed at the diaphyseal cortex where the expanding tumor elevates the periosteum is termed:
explanation: As an aggressive intramedullary osteosarcoma breaks through the cortex, it lifts the periosteum away from the bone shaft; osteogenic cells beneath the elevated periosteal edge deposit a wedge-shaped triangle of reactive bone known radiographically as Codman's triangle.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Why do male dogs with a functional estrogen-secreting Sertoli Cell Tumor (commonly in a cryptorchid testicle) develop a fatal, irreversible non-regenerative pancytopenia?
options: Estrogen directly lyses mature circulating erythrocytes via complement fixation
Hyperestrogenism induces trilinear bone marrow hypoplasia/aplasia
Neoplastic Sertoli cells metastasize rapidly to replace 90% of the femoral bone marrow
Estrogen chelates dietary iron and vitamin B12 in the duodenal lumen
explanation: Canine bone marrow hematopoietic stem cells are exquisitely sensitive to high circulating estradiol, which stimulates thymic/stromal release of a myelopoiesis-inhibitory factor; after a brief initial leukocytosis, dogs develop lethal bone marrow aplasia with severe thrombocytopenia, anemia, and leukopenia.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: How are benign 'Perianal (Hepatoid) Gland Adenomas' biologically and clinically differentiated from malignant 'Apocrine Gland Anal Sac Adenocarcinomas' (AGASACA) in dogs?
options: Hepatoid gland adenomas are androgen-dependent tumors of intact aged male dogs that rarely metastasize
Hepatoid gland adenomas occur exclusively in young spayed female dogs and cause severe hypercalcemia
Hepatoid gland adenomas arise inside the anal sac lumen and metastasize early to the sublumbar iliac lymph nodes
Hepatoid gland adenomas are composed of mucin-filled signet-ring cells that require radical pelvic osteotomy
explanation: Perianal (circumanal) glands are modified non-secretory sebaceous glands consisting of eosinophilic polyhedral 'hepatoid' cells rich in androgen receptors; adenomas occur overwhelmingly in intact older male dogs and regress following orchidectomy, whereas AGASACAs arise from apocrine glands of the anal sac wall (often in females) and cause PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia and sublumbar lymph node metastasis.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In dogs, 'Canine Acanthomatous Ameloblastoma' (formerly termed Acanthomatous Epulis) arising from the periodontal ligament/odontogenic epithelium of the rostral mandible is biologically classified as:
options: A viral papilloma that regresses spontaneously within 4 weeks
A highly metastatic malignancy that spreads rapidly to the lungs and liver
Osteolytic in alveolar bone but does not metastasize
A reactive fibrous hyperplasia that never invades the underlying mandibular bone
explanation: Canine acanthomatous ameloblastoma is histologically benign and never metastasizes, yet it behaves as a locally invasive, osteolytic tumor that destroys adjacent alveolar bone of the jaw, requiring wide surgical margins (hemimandibulectomy/maxillectomy) or radiation.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In young horses and dogs, a benign odontogenic tumor of the jaw whose cut surface contains dozens of miniature, malformed tooth-like structures ('denticles') with organized enamel, dentin, cementum, and pulp papillae is a:
explanation: While both complex and compound odontomas are benign hamartomatous lesions containing fully differentiated dental tissues, a Compound Odontoma forms recognizable miniature tooth-like structures (denticles), whereas a Complex Odontoma is a disorganized conglomerate mass of enamel, dentin, and cementum.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In brachycephalic dog breeds (Boxers, Boston Terriers, and Bulldogs), a common intra-axial brain tumor located in the frontal or piriform lobes—displaying a 'fried-egg' cellular appearance (round nuclei with clear perinuclear halos) and a 'chicken-wire' capillary network—is an:
explanation: Oligodendrogliomas are heavily predisposed in brachycephalic dogs (linked to chromosome 26 loci); formalin fixation causes cytoplasmic retraction around uniform round nuclei ('fried-egg' or 'honeycomb' cells) set in a mucinous matrix with delicate branching capillaries ('chicken-wire' vessels).

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Histologically, benign Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors (Schwannomas) are recognized by alternating hypercellular 'Antoni Type A' zones and loose myxoid 'Antoni Type B' zones, within which regimented parallel rows of Schwann cell nuclei palisade around acellular eosinophilic zones termed:
explanation: Verocay bodies are pathognomonic of Schwannomas (neurilemomas): they consist of two parallel palisading rows of elongated Schwann cell nuclei enclosing an acellular eosinophilic zone composed of reduplicated basement membrane and cytoplasmic processes.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In equine Granulosa Cell Tumors (the most common ovarian neoplasm of mares), cut sections typically reveal a polycystic 'honeycomb' structure, and histology often shows follicular granulosa cells arranged radially around central eosinophilic fluid-filled spaces termed:
explanation: Call-Exner bodies—microscopic rosettes of neoplastic granulosa cells arranged radially around a small central cavity containing eosinophilic basement-membrane-like material—are a classic diagnostic feature of granulosa cell tumors.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: A rare malignant skeletal muscle tumor presenting as protruding, grape-like polypoid masses ('botryoid rhabdomyosarcoma') specifically at the urinary bladder trigone and urethra occurs classically in:
options: Geriatric grey horses with dermal melanomatosis
Adult dairy cows grazing bracken fern pastures
Aged castrated male cats with chronic urolithiasis
explanation: Botryoid rhabdomyosarcoma (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) is a distinctive juvenile mesenchymal malignancy arising in the urinary bladder trigone/urethral submucosa of young (<2 years) large-breed female dogs (especially Saint Bernards and Basset Hounds), forming glistening grape-like ('botryoid') masses containing multinucleated strap cells with cross-striations.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Why does a Canine Cutaneous Histiocytoma ('button tumor' of young dogs, derived from epidermal Langerhans cells expressing E-cadherin and CD1a) undergo spontaneous complete regression within 2 to 3 months?
options: Auto-digestion of the tumor mass by mast cell chymase and tryptase
Terminal differentiation of neoplastic Langerhans cells into dead keratin squames
Loss of blood supply due to spontaneous thrombosis of the nutrient dermal artery
Infiltration from the deep dermal base by host cytotoxic CD8+ T-lymphocytes
explanation: Cutaneous histiocytomas express MHC Class I and II and ICAM-1; after 4–8 weeks, they recruit a dense basal band of host cytotoxic CD8+ T-lymphocytes that migrate upward through the tumor and trigger complete apoptotic regression.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Canine Transmissible Venereal Tumor (CTVT / Sticker's sarcoma) is biologically unique in oncology because the neoplastic cells are:
options: Clonally transmissible somatic allografts physically transplanted as living cells across abraded mucosa
Haploid germ cells derived directly from the donor's seminiferous tubules
Newly transformed host B-lymphocytes induced by a canine gammaherpesvirus
Epithelial keratinocytes transformed by Canine Oral Papillomavirus-1
explanation: CTVT (alongside Tasmanian Devil Facial Tumor Disease) is not caused by an infectious virus transforming host cells; instead, the tumor cells themselves are a 11,000-year-old clonal somatic cell line transmitted as a living cellular allograft during mating, evading host rejection by downregulating MHC Class I/II and secreting TGF-β.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Over 80% of grey horses develop dermal melanomas (most commonly under the tail root, perineum, and parotid region) after 15 years of age due to an autosomal dominant 4.6-kb cis-acting duplication in intron 6 of which gene?
explanation: The grey coat color and melanoma predisposition in horses is caused by a 4.6-kb duplication in intron 6 of Syntaxin-17 (STX17), which upregulates STX17 and NR4A3 expression and drives massive proliferation of both follicular melanocytes (exhausting hair pigment) and dermal melanocytes (producing melanomas).

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Following widespread vaccination and testing for Feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV, which historically caused thymic/mediastinal T-cell lymphoma in young cats), what is now the most prevalent anatomical form of lymphoma in older FeLV-negative cats?
explanation: In the post-FeLV vaccination era, alimentary (gastrointestinal) lymphoma—including low-grade small-cell mucosal T-cell lymphoma and high-grade large-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma—accounts for over 50–70% of all feline lymphomas, predominantly in older FeLV-negative cats.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In dogs and cats, acquired paraneoplastic 'Myasthenia Gravis' (presenting with megaesophagus, regurgitation, and exercise-induced muscular weakness) is classically associated with a cranial mediastinal:
explanation: A thymoma is a neoplasm of thymic epithelial cells containing a variable population of maturing non-neoplastic thymocytes; disordered cortical antigen presentation inside the thymoma generates autoantibodies against skeletal muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (myasthenia gravis) in ~30–40% of canine cases.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In German Shepherd dogs, the inherited paraneoplastic/genodermatosis syndrome of 'Nodular Dermatofibrosis' (multiple firm collagenous skin nodules on the limbs) serves as an external marker for bilateral:
explanation: Canine renal cystadenocarcinoma and nodular dermatofibrosis (RCND) in German Shepherds is caused by an autosomal dominant germline mutation in the Folliculin (FLCN) tumor suppressor gene (homologous to human Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome).

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In dogs, 'Superficial Necrolytic Dermatitis' (Hepatocutaneous Syndrome)—characterized by severe crusting footpad hyperkeratosis and a pathognomonic 'red, white, and blue' trilaminar epidermis on histology—is a paraneoplastic manifestation of a pancreatic:
options: Acinar cell Adenocarcinoma releasing systemic lipase
explanation: Hyperglucagonemia from a pancreatic alpha-cell glucagonoma (or impaired hepatic glucagon catabolism) drives relentless hepatic gluconeogenesis that depletes plasma amino acids by >70%, starving epidermal keratinocytes and producing parakeratosis ('red' surface), keratinocyte edema ('white' middle), and basal hyperplasia ('blue' base).

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Paraneoplastic secondary 'Erythrocytosis' (inappropriate absolute polycythemia with packed cell volume exceeding 65% to 75% and normal arterial oxygen saturation) in dogs is most classically caused by autonomous erythropoietin secretion from a:
explanation: Primary renal neoplasms (renal cell carcinoma, renal lymphoma, or renal fibrosarcoma) secrete ectopic erythropoietin (EPO) or induce peritubular hypoxia via compression, stimulating unrestrained bone marrow erythropoiesis.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In dogs and cattle, 'Chemodectoma' (Paraganglioma) is a neuroendocrine neoplasm arising from chemoreceptor cells sensitive to blood pCO2, pO2, and pH, located most commonly at the:
options: Heart base and carotid arterial bifurcation
Pyloric antrum and duodenal Brunner's glands
Pineal gland and roof of the third ventricle
Renal hilus and adrenal zona glomerulosa
explanation: Chemodectomas (non-chromaffin paragangliomas) arise from the aortic body at the base of the heart (within the pericardial sac) and the carotid body; chronic hypoxia in brachycephalic dog breeds (Boxer, Boston Terrier, Bulldog) strongly predisposes to aortic body tumors.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In the classic Berenblum two-stage model of chemical skin carcinogenesis using DMBA (an initiator) and croton oil / TPA (a promoter), which statement accurately contrasts 'Initiation' with 'Promotion'?
options: Promoters alone induce malignant tumors if applied at high doses without any prior initiator
Initiation is rapid, irreversible, and mutational after single exposure, whereas promotion is reversible and requires repeated exposures AFTER initiation
Applying the promoter before the initiator produces the highest yield of malignant carcinomas
Initiation is reversible and non-mutagenic, whereas promotion is irreversible and additive
explanation: Initiation involves a rapid, irreversible, permanent DNA mutation induced by a single dose of a genotoxic electrophile (DMBA); promotion is a non-mutagenic, reversible clonal proliferation of initiated cells that yields tumors only when applied repeatedly AFTER initiation.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Aflatoxin B1 produced by Aspergillus flavus induces hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma in animals and humans by forming bulky DNA adducts that characteristically cause a signature G-to-T transversion mutation at codon 249 of:
explanation: Hepatic cytochrome P450 converts Aflatoxin B1 into the reactive AFB1-8,9-exo-epoxide, which intercalates into DNA and binds guanine bases to induce a signature AGG-to-AGT (arginine-to-serine) transversion at codon 249 of the TP53 tumor suppressor gene.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In dogs, 'Canine Oral Papillomatosis' (multiple cauliflower-like viral warts on the lips and buccal mucosa of puppies under 1 year of age) is histologically characterized in the stratum granulosum by large, clear, vacuolated keratinocytes with eccentric pyknotic nuclei termed:
explanation: Koilocytes ('hollow cells') are the cytopathic hallmark of papillomavirus infection in the upper stratum spinosum and stratum granulosum, showing perinuclear cytoplasmic clearing (halos), coarse keratohyalin granules, and hyperchromatic crinkled nuclei.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In cats, why do 'Feline Solicited/Vaccine-Associated Fibrosarcomas' (Feline Injection-Site Sarcomas) have such a high local recurrence rate (>50%) following conservative marginal surgical excision?
options: They consist entirely of benign lipocytes that cannot be distinguished grossly from subcutis
They extend microscopic finger-like neoplastic projections deep along fascial planes far beyond palpable pseudocapsule
They shed infectious retroviral particles that immediately transform adjacent skeletal muscle fibers
They metastasize via the cerebrospinal fluid before a primary subcutaneous nodule is palpable
explanation: Feline Injection-Site Sarcomas (FISS) are surrounded by a deceptive inflammatory pseudocapsule of macrophages (containing bluish-grey aluminum hydroxide vaccine adjuvant) through which ribbon-like microscopic tongues of pleomorphic fibroblasts infiltrate deep into intermuscular fascia, requiring 3–5 cm lateral margins and 2 fascial planes deep.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: A malignant neoplasm of vascular endothelial cells that forms irregular, anastomosing, blood-filled vascular clefts lined by plump, pleomorphic, hyperchromatic endothelial cells—occurring most commonly in the spleen and right atrium of German Shepherd dogs—is:
explanation: Canine hemangiosarcoma (malignant endothelioma) arises most frequently in the spleen, right auricle/atrium, liver, and dermis of German Shepherds and Golden Retrievers; it forms tortuous, incomplete vascular channels lined by atypical CD31+/vWF+ endothelial cells and ruptures readily to cause fatal hemoperitoneum or cardiac tamponade.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: Among the three primary testicular neoplasms of aged male dogs, which tumor arises from the germinal spermatogenic epithelium of the seminiferous tubules and is histologically distinguished by large polyhedral cells accompanied by multifocal aggregates of mature T-lymphocytes?
explanation: Canine seminomas arise from germ cells of the spermatic epithelium, form glistening grey-white lobulated masses, and display sheets of large polyhedral cells with vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and characteristic perivascular/interstitial nodules of small mature CD8+ T-lymphocytes.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: What is the most common primary intracranial neoplasm in both aged cats and dogs, arising extra-axially from arachnoid cap cells of the meninges and frequently containing whorled spindle cells and calcified psammoma bodies?
explanation: Meningiomas are extra-axial dural-based tumors derived from arachnoid cap cells (mesoderm/neural crest); they are the single most common primary brain tumor in cats (often multiple in the third ventricle/supratentorial meninges) and dogs, compressing rather than invading underlying brain parenchyma.

topic: Veterinary Oncology & Neoplasia
questionText: In sheep and goats, 'Enzootic Nasal Adenocarcinoma'—a contagious papillary adenocarcinoma arising from the secretory serous/mucous Bowman's glands of the ethmoid turbinates—is caused by:
options: Caprine Arthritis Encephalitis Virus (CAEV), a Lentivirus
Enzootic Nasal Tumor Virus (ENTV-1 in sheep
explanation: Enzootic Nasal Tumor Virus (ENTV-1 in sheep and ENTV-2 in goats) is an oncogenic Betaretrovirus closely related to Jaagsiekte Sheep Retrovirus (JSRV) whose envelope glycoprotein directly transforms ethmoidal secretory epithelial cells via the PI3K/AKT and MAPK pathways.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In chickens infected with Gallid alphaherpesvirus 2 (Marek's Disease Virus), although T-lymphocytes in visceral organs and nerves are latently or neoplastically transformed, productive replication of fully enveloped, cell-free infectious virions occurs exclusively in the:
options: Sciatic nerve Schwann cell myelin sheaths
explanation: In Marek's disease, lymphoid and neural infiltrates harbor non-productive cell-associated virus; only the keratinizing epithelium of the feather follicles supports complete lytic replication and shedding of enveloped, cell-free infectious virus in poultry house dust and dander.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: According to the classical Payne and Biggs histological classification of peripheral nerve lesions in Marek's Disease, a 'Type A' nerve lesion is characterized by:
options: Interneuritic inflammatory edema and heavy infiltration of plasma cells and small lymphocytes cells
Fibrinoid necrosis of epineurial arterioles with calcified granulomas cells
Dense neoplastic infiltration of pleomorphic lymphoblasts and Marek's disease cells
Mild scattering of small mature lymphocytes without edema or demyelination cells
explanation: Payne and Biggs classified Marek's peripheral nerve lesions into Type A (proliferative/neoplastic pleomorphic lymphoblasts, basophilic dark 'Marek's disease cells', and demyelination), Type B (inflammatory interneuritic edema with plasma cells and small lymphocytes), and Type C (mild small lymphocytic infiltration).

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In turkeys, ducks, and chickens, infection with Reticuloendotheliosis Virus (REV, an avian Gammaretrovirus) induces T- and B-cell lymphomas, runting, and a characteristic feather developmental abnormality in wing feathers termed:
explanation: 'Nakanuke' (Japanese for 'defective middle') is a pathognomonic feather lesion of Reticuloendotheliosis Virus infection (including REV-contaminated vaccines), in which necrosis of the intermediate layer of the developing feather epidermis causes barbs in the middle portion of primary wing feathers to remain tightly fused to the rachis.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In acute Infectious Bursal Disease (IBD / Gumboro) in 3- to 6-week-old chickens, in addition to bursal edema and thigh muscle hemorrhages, a classic diagnostic gross lesion in the upper digestive tract is:
options: Thick white curd-like pseudomembranes lining the crop mucosa
Pinpoint hemorrhages exclusively on the tips of proventricular glands
Deep diphtheritic button ulcers around the cecal tonsils
A sharp transverse band of hemorrhage
explanation: While velogenic Newcastle disease produces pinpoint hemorrhages at the tips of proventricular glands, acute Infectious Bursal Disease (IBD) characteristically produces linear or band-like mucosal hemorrhage specifically at the isthmus/junction between the proventriculus and gizzard.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In broiler chickens aged 2 to 5 weeks, 'Necrotic Enteritis'—characterized by a friable, foul-smelling jejunum and ileum lined by a thick yellowish-brown diphtheritic pseudomembrane ('Turkish towel' appearance)—is mediated primarily by which clostridial toxin?
options: NetB pore-forming toxin of Clostridium perfringens Type / G
Epsilon prototoxin of Clostridium perfringens Type D
explanation: Avian necrotic enteritis is caused by Clostridium perfringens strains carrying the plasmid-borne NetB (Necrotic enteritis B-like) beta-barrel pore-forming toxin (classified as Type G) along with alpha-toxin (phospholipase C), producing confluent coagulative necrosis of the small intestinal villi.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: Fatty Liver Hemorrhagic Syndrome (FLHS) causing sudden death in high-producing caged commercial laying hens is characterized at necropsy by:
options: Complete absence of abdominal fat pad with gelatinous hydropericardium
A shrunken, bronze-green fibrotic liver with multiple caseous granulomas
A dark congested liver studded with depressed yellow 'bull's-eye' target lesions
explanation: FLHS occurs in overweight caged laying hens fed high-energy diets under heat stress; estrogen-driven hepatic lipogenesis produces severe hepatic steatosis (>40–70% dry weight fat), weakening the reticulin framework until hepatic sinusoids rupture and bleed beneath Glisson's capsule into the abdominal cavity.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In young broiler chicks aged 2 to 4 weeks, 'Fatty Liver and Kidney Syndrome' (FLKS)—characterized by sudden hypoglycemic paralysis and pale pink-to-yellow fatty enlargement of the liver and kidneys without hemorrhage—is caused by deficiency of:
explanation: Biotin is the prosthetic group for pyruvate carboxylase, a key enzyme in hepatic gluconeogenesis; in fasted young broilers on wheat-based diets deficient in biotin, failure of gluconeogenesis causes fatal hypoglycemia and mobilization of free fatty acids into the liver, kidneys, and myocardium (FLKS).

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: Because routine aqueous 10% neutral buffered formalin dissolves water-soluble urate crystals from avian tissues, specimens collected to demonstrate monosodium urate tophi in poultry Gout must be fixed in absolute ethyl alcohol and stained by:
explanation: Uric acid and monosodium urate crystals are water-soluble and wash out in aqueous formalin; fixing gouty tissues in absolute ethanol preserves the needle-shaped urate crystals, which reduce silver nitrate to brownish-black metallic silver in De Galantha's stain (and show birefringence under polarized light).

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In chicks suffering from 'Nutritional Encephalomalacia' ('Crazy Chick Disease' due to Vitamin E deficiency), the pathognomonic gross and microscopic brain lesions of ischemic necrosis, petechial hemorrhage, and capillary hyaline thrombosis are localized predominantly in the:
options: Olfactory bulbs and rostral cerebral hemispheres
explanation: In chicks, alpha-tocopherol (Vitamin E) deficiency selectively damages the cerebellar microvasculature; at necropsy the cerebellum is swollen, soft, and studded with petechial hemorrhages and greenish-yellow necrotic areas with capillary fibrin thrombi and loss of Purkinje cells.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In poultry, 'Nutritional Roup' (hypovitaminosis A) is differentiated at necropsy from infectious coryza and fowlpox by the presence of:
options: Concentric yellow-green target-shaped necrotic craters in the liver and ceca
Hemorrhagic plugs obstructing the lower trachea and syrinx
Diffuse bronze-mahogany discoloration of the hepatic parenchyma
Multiple pinhead-sized white pustule-like nodules in mucosal glands of pharynx
explanation: Vitamin A is essential for maintaining mucociliary and glandular columnar epithelium; its deficiency in chickens induces squamous metaplasia and keratin plugging of the submucosal esophageal and pharyngeal glands, forming pathognomonic 1–2 mm white raised keratin nodules alongside ocular caseous exudate and renal urate deposits.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In unhatched chicken embryos from breeder flocks fed a diet deficient in Riboflavin (Vitamin B2), dead-in-shell embryos at 14 to 18 days of incubation exhibit dwarfism, edema, and a pathognomonic feather lesion known as:
explanation: In riboflavin-deficient embryos, the keratin sheath of developing down feathers fails to rupture, forcing the growing feather to coil inside the follicle and form a spherical bulbous swelling on the skin surface ('clubbed down').

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In turkeys, chickens, and ducks, 'Avian Spirochetosis'—transmitted by the soft tick Argas persicus and characterized at necropsy by greenish mucoid diarrhea and a markedly enlarged, mottled 'marbled' spleen with pale ecchymotic/necrotic patches—is caused by:
explanation: Borrelia anserina causes acute septicemic avian spirochetosis; the spleen is markedly enlarged and mottled with pale necrotic zones and subcapsular ecchymoses, and motile spiral bacteria are readily demonstrated in wet blood mounts or silver-stained (Levaditi/Warthin-Starry) spleen sections.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: Why must Dipotassium EDTA be avoided as an anticoagulant when collecting blood for routine hematology from ostriches, crows, cranes, and certain reptiles (where Lithium Heparin is used instead)?
options: EDTA dissolves the nuclei of avian heterophils and lymphocytes
EDTA causes immediate clotting of nucleated thrombocytes within 30 seconds
EDTA chelates iron directly out of avian hemoglobin, turning plasma emerald green
EDTA induces rapid in vitro hemolysis
explanation: While EDTA is the preferred hematological anticoagulant in mammals and domestic chickens, in ostriches, corvids, cranes, and tortoises EDTA damages the erythrocyte membrane and causes severe in vitro cell swelling and hemolysis.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: For accurate determination of Prothrombin Time (PT), Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT), and Westergren ESR, venous blood must be mixed with 3.2% or 3.8% Trisodium Citrate in which exact volumetric ratio of blood to anticoagulant?
options: 19 parts blood to 1 part sodium citrate (19 : 1)
1 part blood to 9 parts sodium citrate (1 : 9)
9 parts blood to 1 part sodium citrate (9 : 1)
4 parts blood to 1 part sodium citrate (4 : 1)
explanation: Coagulation assays require a strict 9:1 ratio (9 volumes of whole blood to 1 volume of 3.2% trisodium citrate) so that adding standardized calcium chloride in the laboratory precisely reverses citrate chelation; underfilling tubes leaves excess free citrate that falsely prolongs PT and aPTT.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: Sodium Fluoride (typically combined with Potassium Oxalate in grey-top tubes) is the specific additive of choice for blood glucose and lactate preservation because fluoride ions inhibit which glycolytic enzyme inside erythrocytes?
explanation: Sodium fluoride complexes with magnesium and phosphate ions to inhibit the glycolytic enzyme Enolase (which converts 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate), halting in vitro glucose consumption by erythrocytes and leukocytes.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: Among healthy domestic mammals, which species exhibits the fastest physiological Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)—often settling 15 to 40 mm in 20 minutes—and which group exhibits an ESR of nearly zero?
options: Horses have fastest ESR; ruminants have ESR of nearly zero
Sheep have the fastest ESR; horses have an ESR of zero
Cattle have the fastest ESR; dogs have an ESR of zero
Cats have the fastest ESR; pigs have an ESR of zero
explanation: Equine erythrocytes have a weak negative surface zeta potential and form prominent physiological rouleaux chains, causing rapid sedimentation; ruminant erythrocytes are small and do not form rouleaux, giving cattle, sheep, and goats an ESR of 0–2 mm/hour even during severe inflammation.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: A dog presents with a Packed Cell Volume (PCV) of 18%, a Hemoglobin concentration of 4.5 g/dL, and a Total Erythrocyte Count of 4.5 million/µL. Using Wintrobe's formulas, what are the dog's MCV and MCHC, and how is this anemia morphologically classified?
options: MCV = 25 fL, MCHC = 40 g/dL — Microcytic Hyperchromic anemia (classic for immune spherocytosis)
MCV = 90 fL, MCHC = 35 g/dL — Macrocytic Normochromic anemia (classic for vitamin B12 deficiency)
MCV = 65 fL, MCHC = 33 g/dL — Normocytic Normochromic anemia (classic for chronic renal failure)
MCV = 40 fL, MCHC = 25 g/dL — Microcytic Hypochromic anemia (classic for chronic iron deficiency)
explanation: MCV = (PCV × 10) / RBC = (18 × 10) / 4.5 = 40 fL (below the canine reference range of 60–77 fL = microcytic); MCHC = (Hb × 100) / PCV = (4.5 × 100) / 18 = 25 g/dL (below 32–36 g/dL = hypochromic). Microcytic hypochromic anemia is pathognomonic for chronic iron deficiency (e.g., chronic hookworm or gastrointestinal bleeding).

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: Why is a peripheral blood reticulocyte count (or polychromasia on Wright-Giemsa smears) completely unhelpful for differentiating regenerative from non-regenerative anemia in Horses?
options: Equine erythrocytes retain their nuclei throughout their entire 140-day lifespan
Equine ribosomal RNA cannot be stained by New Methylene Blue or Brilliant Cresyl Blue
Equine reticulocytes mature completely inside the bone marrow and are never released
Horses store 95% of their reticulocytes inside the hepatic sinusoids
explanation: Unlike dogs, cats, cattle, and pigs, horses do not release reticulocytes from the bone marrow into peripheral blood under any degree of anemia; evaluating erythropoietic regeneration in horses requires a bone marrow aspirate, anisocytosis (increased RDW), or serial MCV increases.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: When evaluating a supravital New Methylene Blue-stained blood film from an anemic Cat, why must only 'aggregate reticulocytes' (and not 'punctate reticulocytes') be counted to assess current active bone marrow regeneration?
options: Punctate reticulocytes are artifactual precipitates caused by EDTA anticoagulation
Punctate reticulocytes represent Heinz bodies formed by feline hemoglobin oxidation
Punctate reticulocytes are actually Howell-Jolly nuclear DNA fragments
explanation: Feline reticulocytes exist in two forms: 'aggregate' (coarse reticular clumps of RNA that mature in <12 hours and indicate active ongoing bone marrow release) and 'punctate' (2–10 discrete RNA dots that linger for 2 weeks due to slow feline splenic clearance).

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: Refractile, eccentric, button-like projections on the erythrocyte margin that stain pale pink on Wright's stain and dark blue on supravital New Methylene Blue ('Heinz bodies' accompanied by eccentrocytes) are classically seen in:
options: Dogs with chronic Ancylostoma hookworm infection
Calves with acute Theileria annulata infection
explanation: Heinz bodies are denatured, oxidized, precipitated globin chains caused by oxidative toxins (n-propyl disulfide in onions/garlic, S-methylcysteine sulfoxide in kale/rape, acetaminophen metabolites in cats lacking glucuronyl transferase, and copper-induced oxidative crisis in sheep).

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: Prominent 'basophilic stippling' (numerous fine-to-coarse dark blue ribosomal RNA granules dispersed throughout erythrocytes on Romanowsky-stained blood films) WITHOUT significant anemia is a pathognomonic hematological clue in dogs for:
options: Acute cyanide poisoning, due to inhibition of mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase
Ethylene glycol poisoning, due to calcium oxalate crystallization
Warfarin rodenticide poisoning, due to inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase
Chronic lead poisoning, due to lead inhibition of erythrocyte pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase
explanation: While basophilic stippling accompanies normal regenerative anemia in ruminants, inappropriate basophilic stippling combined with nucleated RBCs (metarubricytosis) in the absence of severe anemia in dogs is classic for lead poisoning, because lead inhibits pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase (the enzyme that normally degrades ribosomal RNA in maturing RBCs).

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In dogs, endogenous hyperadrenocorticism (Cushing's disease) or exogenous corticosteroid administration produces a characteristic 'Stress Leukogram' consisting of which four leukocyte alterations?
options: Degenerative left shift with myelocytes, lymphocytosis, and basophilia
Mature neutrophilia, lymphopenia, eosinopenia, and monocytosis
Severe panleukopenia affecting all granulocyte and mononuclear lines
explanation: Glucocorticoids induce (1) mature neutrophilia by downregulating endothelial adhesion molecules (shifting neutrophils from the marginal pool to the circulating pool) and delaying apoptosis, (2) lymphopenia by redistributing lymphocytes to lymphoid tissues and lympholysis, (3) eosinopenia by marrow sequestration, and (4) monocytosis (particularly prominent in dogs).

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: By contrast, acute epinephrine release ('Physiological / Excitement Leukocytosis') in a frightened young Cat during venipuncture produces a transient leukogram distinguished from a corticosteroid stress leukogram by marked:
options: Degenerative left shift with toxic Döhle bodies
explanation: In excited cats, catecholamines (epinephrine) increase blood flow and contract smooth muscle in the spleen and lymphatics, flushing both marginated neutrophils and lymphocytes into the central bloodstream to cause a transient mature neutrophilia AND marked lymphocytosis (often 7,000–15,000 lymphocytes/µL).

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: When evaluating acute hepatocellular necrosis in Cattle, Sheep, Goats, and Horses, why is serum Sorbitol Dehydrogenase (SDH) or Glutamate Dehydrogenase (GLDH) measured instead of Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT / SGPT)?
options: ALT is present only in the renal cortex of herbivores
SDH and GLDH are cholestatic membrane enzymes induced by corticosteroids
ALT is rapidly excreted in the bile of ruminants before it can enter plasma
explanation: While ALT (SGPT) is the premier liver-specific cytosolic leakage enzyme in dogs and cats, hepatocytes of cattle, sheep, goats, horses, and pigs contain very little ALT; therefore, liver-specific cytosolic Sorbitol Dehydrogenase (SDH) and mitochondrial Glutamate Dehydrogenase (GLDH) are used to diagnose hepatocellular injury in large animals.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: Uniquely in the Dog (and not in cats, horses, or cattle), chronic exposure to endogenous or exogenous glucocorticoids induces synthesis of a distinct hepatic isoenzyme of which serum enzyme?
explanation: Canine hepatocytes uniquely transcribe a corticosteroid-induced Alkaline Phosphatase (CIALP) gene (actually an intestinal-like ALP glycosylated in the liver) in response to cortisol or prednisolone, which can be differentiated from bone and biliary ALP by heat stability at 65°C or levamisole inhibition.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In Cats, why must even a modest 2- to 3-fold elevation in serum Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) be interpreted as a highly specific indicator of cholestasis or Feline Hepatic Lipidosis?
options: Cats lack Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase (GGT) in their biliary epithelium
Feline ALP is inhibited in vitro by EDTA and bilirubin
Feline hepatocytes contain low baseline ALP
Feline osteosarcoma is the only non-hepatic source of ALP in adult cats
explanation: Feline hepatic ALP has a low tissue concentration and a remarkably short plasma half-life (~6 hours due to lack of sialic acid and rapid renal clearance, vs ~66–70 hours in dogs) and cats lack a steroid-induced ALP isoenzyme; notably, Feline Hepatic Lipidosis causes a dramatic rise in ALP with normal or minimal GGT elevation.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In a horse evaluated after an acute episode of Exertional Rhabdomyolysis ('Tying-up'), how do the serum kinetic profiles of Creatine Kinase (CK) and Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST) compare?
options: CK peaks rapidly at 4 to 6 hours
AST peaks within 2 hours and normalizes in 12 hours, while CK peaks at 7 days
CK is elevated only in hepatic necrosis, whereas AST is strictly muscle-specific
Both CK and AST remain permanently elevated for 6 months after a single muscle cramp
explanation: Creatine Kinase (CK) is strictly muscle-specific, has a very short serum half-life (~2–4 hours in horses), peaks 4–6 hours after myonecrosis, and declines rapidly over 24–48 hours if muscle injury stops; AST (shared by muscle and liver) rises more slowly (peaking at 24–48 hours) and has a long half-life (persisting 1–2 weeks).

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In assessing canine and feline renal function, approximately what percentage of functional nephrons must be lost before (1) Symmetric Dimethylarginine (SDMA) increases, (2) Urine Specific Gravity drops to isosthenuria (1.008–1.012), and (3) Serum Creatinine/BUN increases (azotemia)?
options: SDMA at ~25–40% loss; Isosthenuria at ~66% loss; Creatinine
SDMA at 90% loss; Isosthenuria at 50% loss; Creatinine at 10% loss
SDMA at 10% loss; Isosthenuria at 90% loss; Creatinine at 50% loss
SDMA at 75% loss; Isosthenuria at 75% loss; Creatinine at 25% loss
explanation: SDMA is an early glomerular filtration marker that rises when ~25–40% of nephrons are lost; renal concentrating ability fails (isosthenuria, USG 1.008–1.012) when ~66% (2/3) of nephrons are lost; and serum Creatinine/BUN exceed reference limits (renal azotemia) only after ~75% (3/4) of functional nephrons are lost.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In the qualitative urinalysis or milk test for bovine ketosis, Rothera's nitroprusside test (producing a deep permanganate-purple color) reacts most sensitively with:
options: Beta-hydroxybutyric acid exclusively, ignoring acetoacetate and acetone
Acetoacetic acid, but does NOT react with beta-hydroxybutyric acid
explanation: Sodium nitroprusside in alkaline ammonium sulfate (Rothera's test) reacts specifically with the ketone group of acetoacetate (10–20× more sensitive) and acetone to form a purple complex, whereas beta-hydroxybutyrate lacks a free ketone group and gives a negative Rothera reaction.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In urinalysis of a jaundiced dog, Hay's sulfur flower test—in which finely powdered sulfur sprinkled on the surface of urine sinks to the bottom of the test tube—specifically detects the presence of:
options: Bile salts, which lower urine surface tension
Free hemoglobin dimers from intravascular hemolysis
Urobilinogen oxidized by Ehrlich's aldehyde reagent
explanation: Bile salts (bile acids conjugated with glycine or taurine) are potent amphipathic detergents that reduce the surface tension of urine, causing hydrophobic sulfur powder to sink rather than float on the meniscus (Hay's test).

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: What is the physiological glycoprotein secreted exclusively by epithelial cells of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle that polymerizes in acidic, concentrated tubular filtrate to form the matrix of all urinary casts?
explanation: Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein (uromodulin) is secreted by the thick ascending limb of Henle's loop; under conditions of slow tubular flow, acidity, and high salt/protein concentration, it gels into hyaline casts or traps cells/granules to form cellular, granular, and waxy casts.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: Observation of yellowish-brown spherical urinary crystals bearing irregular thorny projections ('thorn-apple' ammonium biurate crystals) in the urine sediment of a 6-month-old Yorkshire Terrier with postprandial neurological signs is a classic clinical pathology finding for:
explanation: In dogs and cats (excluding Dalmatians and Bulldogs), ammonium biurate ('thorn-apple') crystalluria is strongly associated with congenital portosystemic shunts or severe hepatic cirrhosis, because portal blood bypasses the liver, elevating both blood ammonia and uric acid.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, 'Pandy's test' (adding 1 drop of CSF to 1 mL of saturated aqueous phenol/carbolic acid) yields immediate bluish-white cloudiness when CSF contains elevated levels of:
explanation: Normal CSF has a very low protein concentration (12–40 mg/dL, almost entirely albumin); Pandy's carbolic acid reagent (and Nonne-Apelt ammonium sulfate) precipitates globulins, turning turbid in inflammatory CNS diseases such as canine distemper, FIP, or bacterial meningitis.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: Which specialized histochemical stain (using a copper phthalocyanine dye in alcohol) is the standard neuropathological technique for demonstrating normal myelin sheaths in bright blue while highlighting areas of demyelination as unstained pale zones?
explanation: Luxol Fast Blue binds selectively to the lipoproteins and phospholipids (lecithin/sphingomyelin) of intact myelin sheaths, staining normal white matter deep blue; when counterstained with Cresyl Echt Violet (Klüver-Barrera) or PAS, demyelinating plaques stand out clearly.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: To evaluate collapse or condensation of the delicate Type III collagen (reticulin) architectural framework of hepatic sinusoids and lymph nodes, the diagnostic histochemical method of choice is:
explanation: Reticulin fibers (Type III collagen coated with glycoproteins) are argyrophilic; in Gordon and Sweet's or Gomori's reticulin method, oxidized sections are sensitized with iron alum and impregnated with ammoniacal silver nitrate, which is reduced with formalin to stain reticulin fibers jet-black.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: Which histochemical staining technique is specifically employed to stain arterial elastic laminae and pulmonary elastic fibers jet-black while counterstaining collagen fibers red and muscle/cytoplasm yellow?
explanation: Verhoeff's iron-hematoxylin-iodine solution forms cationic lakes that bind elastin with high affinity (staining elastic fibers jet-black), while Van Gieson's picric acid-acid fuchsin counterstain colors collagen red and muscle/cytoplasm yellow.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: Tissues fixed in Zenker's fluid or B-5 fixative (which contain mercuric chloride) develop diffuse crystalline brown-black 'mercury pigment' artifacts that must be removed from deparaffinized sections before staining by treating slides sequentially with:
options: Acidified potassium permanganate followed by 2% oxalic acid
Saturated alcoholic picric acid followed by 1% hydrochloric acid
Lugol's alcoholic iodine solution followed by 5% aqueous sodium thiosulfate
30% hydrogen peroxide followed by concentrated ammonium hydroxide
explanation: Mercuric chloride crystals in Zenker-fixed tissues are converted by alcoholic iodine (0.5% iodine in 70% ethanol) into soluble mercuric iodide, which is then decolorized and washed away with 5% aqueous sodium thiosulfate.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: Which histochemical stain—utilizing hematoxylin, ferric chloride, and phosphotungstic acid—is classically used to demonstrate both cross-striations in skeletal/cardiac muscle (rhabdomyosarcoma) and polymerized fibrin thrombi in deep dichromatic blue?
explanation: Mallory's PTAH is a polychromatic tungsten-hematoxylin lake that stains fibrin, myofibrillar cross-striations (A- and I-bands), and glial fibers deep blue while staining collagen and bone matrix brick-red/ brownish-red.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In standard veterinary necropsy positioning, why are ruminant carcasses placed in LEFT lateral recumbency whereas equine carcasses are placed in RIGHT lateral recumbency?
options: To keep the heavy left-sided bovine rumen and right-sided equine cecum
Because ruminants lack a pleural mediastinal septum while equines lack a functional gallbladder
To prevent post-mortem gravitational pooling of unclotted blood in the right atrium and jugular vein
Because the bovine spleen lies on the right side while the equine spleen lies on the ventral midline
explanation: Positioning a ruminant in left lateral recumbency rests the voluminous rumen underneath and gives unobstructed access to the abomasum, omasum, liver, gallbladder, right kidney, and intestinal mass on the right side; positioning a horse in right lateral recumbency rests the massive cecum and right colon underneath.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In forensic veterinary necropsy, 'Virchow's technique' of post-mortem evisceration differs from 'Rokitansky's' and 'Letulle's' techniques in that Virchow's method:
options: Removes the entire thoracic, cervical, abdominal, and pelvic viscera en masse as one single block
Leaves all thoracic and abdominal organs permanently inside the carcass without removal
Removes and dissects each individual organ separately one by one
Freezes the entire carcass solid and sections it into 2-cm transverse anatomical slabs
explanation: Virchow's method removes and examines organs individually one by one; Letulle's method removes the cervical, thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic organs en masse as a single block for dissection on the table; Rokitansky's method performs in situ dissection combined with organ block removal.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: During forensic examination of a dead newborn calf or foal to determine whether it was born alive (livebirth) or died in utero (stillbirth), if pulmonary putrefaction makes the hydrostatic lung float test unreliable, which supplemental test ('Breslau's second life test') is performed?
options: Examining the renal medullary pyramids for yellow uric acid infarcts
Ligating and testing whether the stomach and duodenum float in water
Testing whether the femur sinks in saturated copper sulfate solution
Measuring the pH of the anterior chamber aqueous humor with litmus paper
explanation: A live-born neonate swallows air along with saliva during its first gasps and cries, causing the ligated stomach and proximal duodenum to float in water (Breslau's second life test) alongside aerophagia and a thrombus in the umbilical arteries.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In broiler breeder and commercial layer hens, 'Big Liver and Spleen Disease' (Hepatitis-Splenomegaly Syndrome)—characterized by subcapsular hepatic hemorrhage, red fluid in the abdomen, ovarian regression, and amyloid-like hyaline deposits in the liver and spleen—is caused by:
explanation: Avian Hepatitis E Virus (Orthohepevirus B, family Hepeviridae) causes Big Liver and Spleen Disease (BLS) / Hepatitis-Splenomegaly Syndrome in mature hens, producing severe hepatosplenomegaly, hepatic subcapsular hematomas, and deposition of eosinophilic hyaline/amyloid-like material in splenic and hepatic sinusoids.

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In growing chicks, severe crusty scab-like dermatitis at the commissures of the beak, margins of the eyelids (causing the eyelids to stick shut), and plantar surfaces of the feet—without paralysis of the toes—is characteristic of a nutritional deficiency of:
options: Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) or Folic acid (Vitamin B9)
Pantothenic acid (Vitamin B5) or Biotin (Vitamin B7)
explanation: Deficiency of Pantothenic acid (Vitamin B5) or Biotin in young chicks produces a characteristic perioral, palpebral, and plantar hyperkeratotic/crusting dermatitis (pantothenic acid deficiency impacts the mouth corners and eyelids first, whereas biotin deficiency impacts the footpads first).

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: On a canine complete blood count (CBC), a 'Regenerative Left Shift' is hematologically defined by:
options: Presence of hypersegmented neutrophils with 6 to 8 nuclear lobes and macrocytic erythrocytes
Normal or low total leukocyte count in which immature band neutrophils outnumber mature segmented neutrophils
Elevated total leukocyte count with neutrophilia in which mature segmented neutrophils outnumber immature band neutrophils
Extreme lymphocytosis and eosinophilia accompanied by complete absence of segmented neutrophils
explanation: In a Regenerative Left Shift, the bone marrow has had sufficient time and storage reserves to respond vigorously to infection: total WBC and neutrophil counts are elevated, and mature segmented neutrophils still outnumber immature band neutrophils/metamyelocytes (unlike a Degenerative Left Shift).

topic: Avian, Clinical & Necropsy Pathology
questionText: In the clinicopathological classification of cavitary effusions (pleural or peritoneal fluid), a 'Modified Transudate'—typically caused by right-sided congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, or neoplasia—is characterized by:
options: Moderate total protein and moderate nucleated cell count
Total protein below 1.5 g/dL and nucleated cell count below 500 cells/µL
Total protein above 5.5 g/dL and over 50,000 degenerate neutrophils/µL with intracellular bacteria
Milky white turbidity with triglyceride concentration 3 times higher than serum
explanation: A modified transudate begins as a hydrostatic transudate inside high-protein lymphatics/sinusoids (such as hepatic sinusoids in right heart failure) or long-standing effusion, resulting in moderate protein (2.5–5.0 g/dL) and moderate cellularity (1,000–7,000/µL of non-degenerate neutrophils, macrophages, and reactive mesothelial cells).
